Sweedler theory for double categories
Vasileios Aravantinos-Sotiropoulos, Christina Vasilakopoulou

Abstract
. In this work, we establish certain enrichments of dual algebraic structures in the setting of monoidal double categories. In more detail, we obtain a tensored and cotensored enrichment of monads in comonads, as well as a tensored and cotensored enrichment of modules in comodules, under very general conditions on the surrounding double category. These include “monoidal closedness” and “local presentability”, leading classical notions which are here introduced in the double categorical context. Furthermore, we show that in this setting, the actual fibration of modules over monads is itself enriched in the opfibration of comodules over comonads. Applying this abstract double categorical framework to the setting of 𝒱 \mathcal{V} -matrices, one directly obtains a many-object generalization of the known enrichment of modules over monoids in comodules over comonoids in a monoidal category 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , which was originally induced by Sweedler’s measuring k k -coalgebras in vector spaces. In the present setting the result involves 𝒱 \mathcal{V} -enriched modules of 𝒱 \mathcal{V} -categories and 𝒱 \mathcal{V} -enriched comodules of 𝒱 \mathcal{V} -cocategories.



1.
Introduction

Sweedler’s measuring coalgebras
[
Swe69
]
were the starting point for establishing a framework in which dual algebraic structures like algebras and coalgebras, modules and comodules
in monoidal categories are enriched in one another. In more detail, for two
k
-algebras
A
and
B
, their universal measuring
k
-coalgebra
P(A,B)
is defined via the property that any
k
-coalgebra map
C\to P(A,B)
bijectively corresponds, in a natural way, to a
k
-algebra map
A\to\mathrm{Hom}_{k}(C,B)
into the convolution
k
-algebra. Already part of folklore for the category of vector spaces, and formally obtained in
[
Vas12
,
HLFV17a
]
in any symmetric monoidal closed and locally presentable category
\mathcal{V}
, universal measuring comonoids are the hom-objects of an enrichment of monoids in comonoids which is furthermore tensored and cotensored – see also
[
Fox67
]
. Notably,
[
AJ13
]
studies the special case of differential graded vector spaces in an effort to approach Koszul duality for (co)algebras
[
LV07
]
, and exhibits how various functors involved in the enrichment (collectively called
Sweedler theory
) relate to the bar-cobar adjunctions.

On the other hand, measuring comodules
[
Bat00
]
are defined in an analogous way to measuring coalgebras: for two
k
-modules
M,N
and a
k
-comodule
X
, we have a natural bijection between
k
-module morphisms
M\to\mathrm{Hom}_{k}(X,N)
and
k
-comodule morphisms
X\to Q(M,N)
into the universal measuring
k
-comodule of
M
and
N
. These are also the hom-objects of a tensored and cotensored enrichment of a (global) category of modules over monoids in a category of comodules over comonoids
[
HLFV17b
]
, under the same assumptions on the ambient monoidal category as before. Moreover, the natural structures of fibration of modules over monoids and opfibration of comodules over comonoids are compatible with said enrichments, providing an illustative example of an enriched fibration structure
[
Vas18
]
.
Pictorially,

(1)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Mod}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Comod}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Alg}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Coalg}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{enriched}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{fibred}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{opfibred}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{enriched}}

In
[
Vas19
]
, a double categorical framework is proposed as the appropriate one for generalizing Sweedler theory for (co)algebras to its many-object setting.
More specifically, it is shown therein that
\mathcal{V}
-categories are tensored and cotensored enriched in a category of
\mathcal{V}
-
cocategories
– structures equipped with cocomposition
arrows of the form
C(x,z)\to\sum_{y}C(x,y)\otimes C(y,z)
, which are also of independent interest
[
Kel06
]
. These results manifest themselves in a double category of enriched matrices
\mathbb{D}=\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
(e.g.
[
BCSW83
]
for the corresponding bicategory), using double categorical monads (
[
FGK11
]
) which in this case are precisely
\mathcal{V}
-enriched categories. In the general setting, an enrichment of monads in an appropriate category of
comonads
is therein established when
\mathbb{D}
is a monoidal, fibrant (
[
Shu08
]
) and moreover
locally closed monoidal
double category – asking that
\mathbb{D}_{0}
and
\mathbb{D}_{1}
are monoidal closed in a coherent way.
This story ultimately results in an enriched fibration

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Cat}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Cocat}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Set}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Set}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{enriched}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{fibred}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{opfibred}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{enriched}}

where the bottom arrow is simply due to the cartesian closure of
\mathsf{Set}
.

The present paper began as a natural continuation of the many-object generalization of Sweedler theory, now for modules and comodules. The end result concerns
\mathcal{V}
-modules for
\mathcal{V}
-categories in two flavors, both special cases of classical
\mathcal{V}
-bimodules
[
Law73
]
. One the one hand, one-sided single-indexed
\mathcal{V}
-modules
M
of
\mathcal{V}
-categories
A
, equipped with action arrows of the form
A(x,y)\otimes M(y)\to M(x)
for all
x,y\in\mathrm{obj}(A)
; these are (
A
,
\mathbf{1}
)-bimodules for
\mathbf{1}
the terminal category. On the other hand, one-sided double-indexed
\mathcal{V}
-modules of
\mathcal{V}
-categories, equipped with action arrows of the form
A(x,y)\otimes M(y,z)\to M(x,z)
for all
x,y\in\mathrm{obj}(A)
and
z\in Z
for some set
Z
; these are (
A
,
\mathrm{disc}(Z)
)-bimodules for
\mathrm{disc}(Z)
the discrete
\mathcal{V}
-category on the set
Z
.
Such structures naturally arise as particular instances, in
\mathbb{D}=\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
, of the newly introduced
modules
in double categories.
We note that, although
bimodules
in fibrant double categories were considered e.g. in
[
Shu08
, Sec. 11]
, we here investigate one-sided modules as the analogue for modules over monoids in a monoidal category.

What started as developing the next many-object step, eventually led to a reexamination and reworking of the framework of the earlier
[
Vas19
]
. Indeed, our first main result (
Theorem

3.4.12
) establishes a tensored and cotensored enrichment of monads in comonads in a double category under broader and more natural assumptions than the earlier version
[
Vas19
, Thm. 3.24]
, which had two technical conditions needed to be checked by hand in each specific double category of interest. To that end, current
Proposition

3.3.13
confirms that a certain internal hom-induced functor preserves cartesian liftings in any
monoidal closed
1
1

1

“Locally” is henceforth dropped from our terminology, and the definition is also slightly altered – see
Definition

3.2.9
and surrounding discussion.
double category, resolving the first technical condition. Furthermore, by introducing the notion of a
locally presentable
(fibrant) double category in
Section

3.4
, various ordinary categories involved in the theory end up being locally presentable which in paricular resolves the second condition.

This results in a more efficient and theoretically elegant high-level approach, where general conditions on the double category replace more specialized ones which involve performing technical calculations in each example application. Moreover, and perhaps more importantly, the notions of monoidal closed and locally presentable categories both constitute central and well-studied properties in the context of ordinary category theory. It is therefore natural to expect that double-categorical counterparts, such as the ones introduced herein, will play a significant role in the development of double category theory and lead to applications in their own right, independently of our current storyline.

Back to Sweedler theory, the second main result of the paper (
Theorem

4.2.4
) establishes, in a very analogous spirit, a tensored and cotensored enrichment of modules in comodules in a double category which is fibrant, braided monoidal closed and locally presentable. Moreover, under the same assumptions on
\mathbb{D}
, the fibration of modules over monads
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
is enriched in the monoidal opfibration of comodules over comonads
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})
, settling the analogue of
1
from monoidal to double categories. As a special case of this theorem, for
\mathbb{D}=\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
we obtain an enrichment of the fibration of
\mathcal{V}
-modules over
\mathcal{V}
-categories in the opfibration of
\mathcal{V}
-comodules over
\mathcal{V}
-cocategories. We note that the desired enrichments in the general double categorical setting are induced via
actions
of monoidal categories, using standard results originating from an equivalence between “closed representations” and tensored enriched categories
[
GP97
]
.
Naturally, before reaching the final enrichment result, the general theory of the newly introduced modules and comodules in double categories is developed: particular emphasis is given to (co)monadicity results (
Proposition

4.1.7
) and (op)fibration structures (
Propositions

4.1.10
and
4.1.12
), as well as monoidality (
Propositions

4.1.20
and
4.1.24
) and local presentability of certain fibers (
Proposition

4.1.18
). We mention in passing that local presentability of categories of (co)monads and (co)modules in double categories are part of ongoing work in progress.

Finally, it should be stressed that such a thorough development of the theory regarding enrichment of (co)monads and (co)modules in double categories is of course anticipated to be applied to different settings as well, by changing the surrounding double category.
One example of interest is the fruitful context of operads and their modules, which is part of ongoing work in progress
[
GGV24
]
. Considering the double category
\mathbb{D}=\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}
of
\mathcal{V}
-
symmetric sequences
whose monads are colored symmetric
\mathcal{V}
-operads
[
GJ17
]
, one can obtain similar enrichment results that involve (co)operads and their (co)modules – broadly in a direction that analogously approaches bar-cobar duality for operads using abstract machinery
[
AJ14
]
.
One particular point, however, that shows that this shall not be a mere application of
Theorems

3.4.12
and
4.2.4
is that the double category
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}
does not satisfy all assumptions: for example, it is an
oplax monoidal
rather than monoidal double category, by
[
GGV24
, Thm. 10.9]
. Thus, the general theory needs to be appropriately adjusted to cover richer examples, which is planned as future work.

Outline

Section

2
covers preliminaries which are largely known results, with certain convenient reformulations.

Section

3
contains some background on double categories, and revisits the context of monads and comonads but in a broader setting than
[
Vas19
]
. New material
includes parallel limits and colimits (
Definition

3.1.9
), monoidal closed double categories (
Definition

3.2.9
and related theory), locally presentable double categories and the enrichment of monads in comonads (
Section

3.4
and preceding results from
Section

3.3
). Finally,
Section

4
contains new material and develops the theory of modules and comodules in double categories, reaching the tensored and cotensored enrichment of modules in comodules.

2.
Preliminaries

In this section, we recall some known concepts and constructions that will be needed in what follows, drawn from various relevant topics such as
monads and modules in bicategories, enrichment, fibrations and the so-called Sweedler theory for monoidal categories. The purpose is to make the material as self-contained
as possible, providing references for further reading wherever appropriate.

2.1.
Monads and modules

We assume that the reader is familiar with the basic theory of bicategories, see e.g.
[
Bén67
,
KS74
]
, as well as monoidal categories, see
e.g.
[
JS93a
]
. We first recall the notions of (co)monads and their (co)modules in a bicategory.

.

A
monad
in a bicategory
\mathcal{K}
consists of an object
X
together with an endomorphism

a:X\to X
and 2-cells
\eta:1_{X}\Rightarrow a
,
\mu:a\circ a\Rightarrow a
called the
unit
and
multiplication
,
such that the following diagrams commute:

A
(lax) monad functor
between two monads
a:X\to X
and
b:Y\to Y
in a bicategory
\mathcal{K}

consists of a 1-cell
f:X\to Y
between the 0-cells of the monads together with a 2-cell
bf\Rightarrow fa

satisfying compatibility conditions with multiplications and units.

Together with the appropriate transformations between lax monad functors, we have the bicategory
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathcal{K})
of all monads in
\mathcal{K}
. Any
lax functor between bicategories
F\colon\mathcal{K}\to\mathcal{L}
induces a lax functor
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathcal{K})\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathcal{L})
, or in other words lax functors
preserve monads. One way of explaining this is to observe that a monad in
\mathcal{K}
can be equivalently described as a lax functor

\bf{1}\to\mathcal{K}
, where
\bf{1}
is the terminal bicategory with a unique object – and
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathcal{K})
is in fact
[\mathbf{1},\mathcal{K}]_{\mathrm{lax}}
.

Definition 2.1.2
.

Let
(a\colon X\to X,\eta,\mu)
be a monad in the bicategory
\mathcal{K}
. A
(left) module
over
a
consists of a 1-cell
m\colon U\rightarrow X
and a 2-cell
\lambda\colon a\circ m\Rightarrow m
such that the following diagrams commute:

A
morphism
of left
a
-modules
(m,\lambda)\rightarrow(m^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime})
with domain
U
is a 2-cell
\alpha\colon m\Rightarrow m^{\prime}
such that the
diagram below commutes:

\textstyle{a\circ m\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\circ\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\lambda}
\textstyle{a\circ m^{\prime}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\lambda^{\prime}}
\textstyle{m\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\alpha}
\textstyle{m^{\prime}}

We thus have for any given object
U\in\mathcal{K}
a
category of (left)
a
-modules
with domain
U
, denoted by
{}_{a}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}
.
In the classical case
\mathcal{K}=\mathsf{Cat}
, modules over a monad

T:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}
with domain the terminal category
\bf{1}
are the usual ‘
T
-algebras’ in the literature – and the category

{}_{T}^{\bf{1}}\mathsf{Mod}
is just the Eilenberg-Moore category
\mathcal{C}^{T}
.

Remark 2.1.3
.

A more compact description of the category of left
a
-modules of given domain
U
, for a monad
a\colon X\rightarrow X
in the bicategory
\mathcal{K}
, is as follows. For any object
U\in\mathcal{K}
there is an induced monad (in the ordinary sense) on the hom-category
\mathcal{K}(U,X)
given by post-composition

\mathcal{K}(U,a)\colon\mathcal{K}(U,X)\rightarrow\mathcal{K}(U,X)

Then
{}_{a}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}
is precisely the Eilenberg-Moore category
\mathcal{K}(U,X)^{\mathcal{K}(U,a)}
of
\mathcal{K}(U,a)
-algebras.

There are also the dual concepts of
comonads

(c\colon Z\to Z,\delta,\epsilon)
and (left)
c
-
comodules

(k\colon V\to Z,\gamma\colon k\Rightarrow c\circ k)
forming appropriate categories

{}_{c}^{V}\mathsf{Comod}
which is the category of Eilenberg-Moore coalgebras
\mathcal{K}(V,Z)_{\mathcal{K}(V,c)}
for the comonad given by post-composition with
c
.

Next, we recall some basic facts regarding monoids and comonoids in monoidal categories.
These can be
viewed as the one-object case of the above notions, since if
\mathcal{K}
is a bicategory with a single object
*
, it is equivalent to the data of a
monoidal category
\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{K}(*,*)
with tensor corresponding to composition
\mathcal{K}(*,*)\times\mathcal{K}(*,*)\rightarrow\mathcal{K}(*,*)
. A monad is
then just an object
A\in\mathcal{V}
together with morphisms
\mu\colon A\otimes A\to A
,
\eta\colon I\to A
satisfying associativity and unit laws, i.e.
a
monoid
. Dually,
comonoids

(C,\delta\colon C\to C\otimes C,\epsilon\colon C\to I)
can be viewed as comonads therein.

Along with the corresponding notions of morphism, we have the categories
\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V})
and
\mathsf{Comon}(\mathcal{V})
. Note that if
\mathcal{V}
is braided
monoidal, then both categories are themselves monoidal, although not necessarily braided. If however
\mathcal{V}
is symmetric, then symmetry is
inherited by both
\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V})
and
\mathsf{Comon}(\mathcal{V})
.

Analogously to how lax functors between bicategories preserve monads, any lax monoidal functor
F\colon\mathcal{V}\to\mathcal{W}
with
structure maps
\phi_{A,B}\colon FA\otimes FB\to F(A\otimes B)
and
\phi_{0}\colon I\to F(I)
induces a functor between their categories of monoids

(2)

\mathsf{Mon}F\colon\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V})\to\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{W})

explicitly given by
(A,\mu,\eta)\mapsto(FA,F\mu\circ\phi_{A,A},F\eta\circ\phi_{0})
. Dually, oplax monoidal functors induce functors between the
categories of comonoids. We usually denote
\mathsf{Mon}F
and
\mathsf{Comon}F
with the same name
F
in order to not overburden with notation.

Briefly recall that a functor
F\colon\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
of two variables has a
(right) parameterized
adjoint when for all

B\in\mathcal{B}
,
F(\textrm{-},B)\dashv R(B,\textrm{-})
; in particular this gives rise to a functor
R\colon\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{A}
, see

[
ML98
, §IV.7,Thm. 3]
.
When
\mathcal{V}
is braided monoidal closed, the internal hom functor
[\textrm{-},\textrm{-}]\colon\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{V}\to\mathcal{V}
obtains a lax monoidal structure, as
the parameterized adjoint to the strong monoidal tensor functor, see e.g.
[
HLFV17a
, Prop. 2.1]
.
As a result, there is an induced functor between categories of monoids which is denoted

(3)

[\textrm{-},\textrm{-}]\colon\mathsf{Comon}(\mathcal{V})^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V})\to\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V}).

This says that for a comonoid
C
and a monoid
A
in a braided monoidal closed category
\mathcal{V}
, the object
[C,A]
has the standard
convolution
monoid structure.

Specializing the notion of module over a monad in a bicategory, a (left)
module
over a monoid
A
in
\mathcal{V}
consists of a pair
(M,\lambda)
, where
\lambda:A\otimes M\rightarrow M
is an
action
of
A
on
M
, i.e. satisfies standard compatibilities with the multiplication and unit. Similarly, a module morphism
(M,\lambda)\rightarrow(M^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime})
is now an arrow
f:M\rightarrow M^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}
which commutes with the actions; thus we obtain the category
\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{V}}(A)
of
A
-modules in
\mathcal{V}
.
Dually, we have the category
\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}(C)
of (left)
C
-comodules

(K,\gamma\colon K\to C\otimes K)
over a comonoid
C
in

\mathcal{V}
.
By
Remark

2.1.3
, we obtain the well-known fact that the categories
\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{V}}(A)
and
\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}(C)
are respectively monadic and comonadic over
\mathcal{V}
, e.g. via the monad
(A\otimes\textrm{-},\mu\otimes\textrm{-},\eta\otimes\textrm{-})
.

Any lax monoidal functor
F\colon\mathcal{V}\to\mathcal{W}
also induces a functor between categories of modules

\mathsf{Mod}F\colon\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{V}}(A)\to\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{W}}(FA)

for any monoid
A
, mapping
(M,\lambda)
to
(FM,F\lambda\circ\phi_{A,M})
.
As a particular instance, the lax monoidal internal hom
[\textrm{-},\textrm{-}]\colon\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{V}\to\mathcal{V}
for a braided monoidal closed category induces, further to
3
, a functor

(4)

[\textrm{-},\textrm{-}]_{CA}\colon\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}(C)^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{V}}(A)\to\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{V}}([C,A])

for any comonoid
C
and monoid
A
.
To put the action of this functor in more concrete terms, given any
C
-comodule
(K,\gamma)
and any
A
-module
(M,\lambda)
,
[K,M]
acquires a

[C,A]
-module structure whose action
[C,A]\otimes[K,M]\to[K,M]
is defined as the transpose of the following composite under the
adjunction
-\otimes K\dashv[K,-]:

(5)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[C,A]\otimes[K,M]\otimes K}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[C,A]\otimes[K,M]\otimes C\otimes K}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[C,A]\otimes C\otimes[K,M]\otimes K}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\otimes M}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1\otimes\gamma}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{ev}\otimes\mathrm{ev}}

Up to this point, we have recalled the definitions of categories of (co)modules over a
fixed
(co)monoid. We now turn to ‘global’ categories of (co)modules, fundamental in this work, by also summarizing the main points of
[

, § 4.1]
.

Definition 2.1.4

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda}

Dually, the

\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}
has objects all comodules
K

in
\mathcal{V}
, and a morphism

is a comonoid morphism

and an arrow

making the dual diagram to the above commute.

There are obvious forgetful functors
\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V})
and
\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathsf{Comon}(\mathcal{V})
which map

states that (co)limits in the respective global categories are created from those in
\mathcal{V}
and (co)monoids.

Proposition 2.1.5
.

The functor
\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathcal{V}\times\mathsf{Comon}(\mathcal{V})
which maps
K_{C}
to the pair
(K,C)
is comonadic, with right adjoint

(Y,D)\mapsto(D\otimes Y)_{D}
. Dually, the global category of modules
\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{V}}
is monadic over the category
\mathcal{V}\times\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V})
.

Let us also record here that, as was the case for the categories of monoids and comonoids in
\mathcal{V}
, the existence of a braiding on
\mathcal{V}
implies
that the global categories
\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{V}}
and
\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}
have a monoidal structure which furthermore is symmetric whenever
\mathcal{V}
is such. For
example,
X_{C}\otimes Y_{D}
is a
C\otimes D
-comodule with coaction

X\otimes Y\xrightarrow{\delta\otimes\delta}X\otimes C\otimes Y\otimes D\xrightarrow{1\otimes s\otimes 1}X\otimes Y\otimes C\otimes D.

Finally, in what follows we are in particular interested in local presentability of categories of (co)monoids and (co)modules. For the
general theory of locally presentable and accessible categories, we refer the reader to
[
MP89
,
AR94
]
.
Briefly recall that if
\lambda
is a regular cardinal, a
\lambda
-
accessible
category is a category with
\lambda
-filtered colimits
and a small set of
\lambda
-presentable objects (namely
\mathcal{C}(c,\textrm{-})
preserves
\lambda
-filtered colimits) such that every other object is a

\lambda
-filtered colimit of those; and a category is
locally

\lambda
-
presentable
if it is furthermore cocomplete. A
locally
presentable
category is locally
\lambda
-presentable for some
\lambda
.

The following theorem ensures that any cocontinuous functor on a locally presentable
category has a right adjoint, since presentable objects form a small dense subcategory.

Theorem 2.1.6
.

[
Kel05
, Thm. 5.33]

If the cocomplete category
\mathcal{C}
has a small dense subcategory, every cocontinuous
S\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}
has a right adjoint.

For example, the above can be used to deduce monoidal closedness of comonoids when
\mathcal{V}
is closed (see
[
Por08
, § 3.2]
),
because
\mathsf{Comon}(\mathcal{V})
– as well as
\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V})
– is locally presentable under the conditions below.

Proposition 2.1.7
.

If
\mathcal{V}
is a locally presentable monoidal category where
\otimes
preserves filtered colimits in both variables, the category of monoids

\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V})
is locally presentable and finitary monadic over
\mathcal{V}
and the category of comonoids
\mathsf{Comon}(\mathcal{V})
is locally presentable and
comonadic over
\mathcal{V}
. Moreover, if
\mathcal{V}
is braided monoidal closed, then
\mathsf{Comon}(\mathcal{V})
is monoidal closed.

Briefly, both categories can be written using 2-categorical limits (e.g. inserters and equifiers) of locally presentable categories and (accessible) functors,
thus they end up locally presentable essentially due to the “Limit Theorem” for accessible categories
[
MP89
, Thm. 5.1.6]
;
more explicit descriptions of these constructions for comonoids can be found in
[
Por08
]
.

Similarly, local presentability is also inherited by categories of modules and comodules as a result of their (co)monadic structure over
\mathcal{V}
.
This follows from
[
AR94
, § 2.78]
for Eilenberg-Moore algebras and an analogous argument for coalgebras again as a result of the Limit Theorem for accessible categories, and the fact that a category is locally
presentable if and only if it is cocomplete and accessible category or equivalent a complete and accessible
[
AR94
, Cor. 2.47]
.

Theorem 2.1.8
.

For a locally presentable category
\mathcal{V}
, the category of algebras for a finitary monad as well as the category of coalgebras for a finitary comonad are locally presentable categories.

For example, under the assumptions below, the respective (co)monads preserve all filtered colimits.

Proposition 2.1.9
.

If
\mathcal{V}
is a locally presentable monoidal category where
\otimes
preserves filtered colimits in both variables, the category of modules

\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{V}}(A)
for any monoid
A
and the category of comodules
\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}(C)
for any comonoid
C
are locally presentable.
Moreover, the global category of modules

\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{V}}
and the global category of comodules
\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}
are locally presentable.

2.2.
Fibrations

In this section we record some definitions and results involving fibred adjunctions and fibred limits; this is done to fix notation and for
future reference. For further details and related bibliography, we refer the reader to
[
Her94
,
HLFV17b
]
.

Briefly recall that
P\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{X}
is a (cloven)
fibration
if for any
f\colon X\to Y
in
\mathcal{X}
(called the
base
) and
B
above
Y
in
\mathcal{A}
(called the
total
category), there is a cartesian lifting
\mathrm{Cart}(f,B)\colon f^{*}B\to B
of
f
to
B
, namely any other map
u\colon A\to B
with
Pu=f\circ g
uniquely factorizes through
\mathrm{Cart}(f,B)
via some
v\colon A\to f^{*}B
with
Pv=g
.
The
fibre
category
\mathcal{A}_{Y}
consists of objects above
Y
and morphisms above
1_{Y}
(called
vertical
). By the universal
property of liftings, there are induced
reindexing
functors
f^{*}\colon\mathcal{A}_{Y}\to\mathcal{A}_{X}
for any
f
in the base, satisfying

(g\circ f)^{*}\cong g^{*}\circ f^{*}
and
1_{\mathcal{A}_{X}}\cong(1_{X})^{*}
. If these isomorphisms are equalities, we have a
split
fibration.
Dually, we have the notion of an
opfibration
with cocartesian liftings deloned
\mathrm{Cocart}(f,A)\colon A\to f_{!}A
. A
bifibration
is both a fibration and an opfibration,
equivalently we have adjunctions
f_{!}\dashv f^{*}
.

The fundamental
Grothendieck construction
provides a passage between fibrations
\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{X}
and pseudofunctors

\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathsf{Cat}
. Concretely, given a pseudofunctor
F\colon\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathsf{Cat}
, its
Grothendieck category

\int F
has as objects pairs
(X\in\mathcal{X},A\in FX)
and as morphisms pairs
(f\colon X\to Y\in\mathcal{X},\phi\colon A\to f^{*}B\in FX)
. Essentially, the induced fibration
\int F\to\mathcal{X}
that maps
(X,A)
to
X
has as fibres the categories
FX
and and as reindexing functors
Ff\colon FY\to FX
.
This construction extends to a 2-equivalence between the corresponding 2-categories;
for example, a fibred 1-cell between two fibrations
P,Q
is a commutative

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}

where
K
preserves cartesian liftings. In the split case, the correspondence restricts to ordinary functors into
\mathsf{Cat}
. Similarly, there is an equivalence between opfibrations and pseudofunctors
\mathcal{X}\to\mathsf{Cat}
.

As an example, consider the global categories of (co)modules of

. These are split fibred and

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Cat}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Gi}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Lim}PG}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces PGi}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{i}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cart}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\kappa_{i}}

It can be checked that

(\mathrm{Cart}(\kappa_{i},Gi)\circ p_{i}\colon A\to Gi)_{i\in\mathcal{I}}
gives the desired limit of
G
in
\mathcal{A}
, and clearly

.
∎

As is evident from the above constructions, when both exist, limits inside the fibers do not need to coincide with limits in the total category in
general; one case this is true is that of connected limits.

Corollary 2.2.3
.

Let
\mathcal{I}
be a small connected category and
P\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{X}
a fibration such that
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{X}
have,

preserves all

\mathcal{I}
-limits. For every
X\in\mathcal{X}
, the inclusion
\mathcal{A}_{X}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{A}
preserves
\mathcal{I}
-limits.

Proof.

Consider a diagram
G\colon\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{A}_{X}
. Since
\mathcal{I}
is connected, the limit of

\mathcal{I}\xrightarrow{G}\mathcal{A}_{X}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{A}\xrightarrow{P}\mathcal{X}
is now (isomorphic to)
X
, since
PG
is the constant diagram on
X
. More
precisely, in the picture of
9
there exists an isomorphism

in
\mathcal{X}
, which is forced to be
\Delta
by the
uniqueness of the triangle commutativities. Since
\Delta
is invertible, its cartesian lift

\mathrm{Cart}(\Delta,\mathrm{Lim}G)
is also invertible in
\mathcal{A}
, which proves the result.
∎

2.3.
Sweedler theory for monoidal categories

In this section, we summarize the main points regarding an enrichment of monoids in comonoids using Sweedler’s
universal
measuring coalgebras

[
Swe69
]
, an enrichment of the global category of modules in comodules using
universal measuring comodules

[
Bat00
]
, as well as an enriched fibration structure they form. The term ‘Sweedler
theory’ was originally used in
[
AJ13
]
for the theory surrounding the enrichment of dg-(co)algebras specifically, but here we use it
as an umbrella term for general (co)monoids, (co)modules and their (op)fibrations –

Theorems

2.3.2
,
2.3.5
and
2.3.14
.
More details on this material can be found in
[
HLFV17a
,
HLFV17b
,
Vas18
]
.

Recall that an
action

[
Bén67
]
of a monoidal category
(\mathcal{V},\otimes,I)
on an ordinary category
\mathcal{C}
is a functor

*\colon\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}
along with isomorphisms

(11)

\chi_{X,Y,C}\colon X*(Y*C)\cong(X\otimes Y)*C\textrm{ and }\nu_{C}\colon C\cong I*C

satisfying compatibility conditions that express, on higher level, that
\mathcal{C}
is a pseudomodule for the pseudomonoid
\mathcal{V}
in the
cartesian monoidal 2-category
\mathsf{Cat}
. If
*
is an action, then
*^{\mathrm{op}}
is also an action. There is a connection between
\mathcal{V}
-actions and

\mathcal{V}
-enrichment, which e.g. in
[
JK02
]
is stated as follows:
if a monoidal category
\mathcal{V}
acts on a category
\mathcal{C}
where the action has a parameterized adjoint, then we can enrich
\mathcal{C}
in

\mathcal{V}
. The following version is
[
LFV20
, Prop. 7]
, and starts from an action of the opposite
of a braided monoidal category and is more convenient for our purposes.

Theorem 2.3.1
.

Suppose
\mathcal{V}
is a braided monoidal category, and
\pitchfork\colon\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}
is an action with an adjoint
\textrm{-}\pitchfork^{\mathrm{op}}D\dashv R(\textrm{-},D)
via
\mathcal{C}(C,X\pitchfork D)\cong\mathcal{V}(X,R(C,D))
. Then there is a
\mathcal{V}
-enriched category with hom-objects
R(C,D)
and underlying category
\mathcal{C}
.

Moreover, if
\mathcal{V}
is closed then the enriched category admits cotensors
X\pitchfork C
. Finally, if the action has another parameterized adjoint
X*\textrm{-}\dashv X\pitchfork\textrm{-}
then it also admits tensors
X*C
.

The above theory can be applied to the categories of monoids and comonoids in a symmetric
3
3

3

Symmetry is needed because braiding alone only makes the category of comonoids monoidal.

monoidal closed
\mathcal{V}
which is furthermore locally presentable.
More precisely, under these assumptions,
\mathsf{Comon}(\mathcal{V})
is a symmetric monoidal closed category (
Proposition

2.1.7
) and the restricted
internal hom
[\textrm{-},\textrm{-}]\colon\mathsf{Comon}(\mathcal{V})^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V})\to\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V})
of
3
is an action with adjoints

(12)

\displaystyle[\textrm{-},B]^{\mathrm{op}}\dashv P(\textrm{-},B)\colon

\displaystyle\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V})^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathsf{Comon}(\mathcal{V})

(13)

\displaystyle C\triangleright\textrm{-}\dashv[C,\textrm{-}]\colon

\displaystyle\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V})\to\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V})

using local presentability and (co)continuity properties and
Theorem

2.1.6
appropriately, as detailed in
[
HLFV17a
, § 4&5]
. Thus the above theorem applies,
where the hom-objects
R(A,B)
are the universal measuring comonoids first introduced in
[
Swe69
]
in the context of vector
spaces.

Theorem 2.3.2

(Sweedler theory for (co)monoids)
.

Suppose
\mathcal{V}
is a locally presentable, symmetric monoidal closed category. The category of monoids
\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V})
is tensored and cotensored enriched in the symmetric monoidal closed category of comonoids
\mathsf{Comon}(\mathcal{V})
.

The situation for (co)modules is similar. Although it is still possible (yet less informative, see
[
HLFV17b
, Rem. 4.8]
) to obtain required adjunctions using results
like

, it is more efficient to use the theory of (op)fibred adjunctions.
First of all, under the running assumptions on

, the
category of comodules is monoidal closed as shown in
[

, Prop. 4.5]
; below is a sketch of the argument, which is later
generalized in

.

Proposition 2.3.3
.

For a braided monoidal closed and locally presentable category

, the monoidal category
\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}
is closed.

Sketch.

The existence of the internal hom of

follows from

as an adjoint of the opfibred 1-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Comon}(\mathcal{V})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textrm{-}\otimes X_{C}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bot}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\textsc{Hom}}(X_{C},\textrm{-})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textrm{-}\otimes C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bot}

where the bottom adjunction is the monoidal closed structure of

from

∎

Moreover, the restricted internal hom

.

Suppose

All clauses of
Theorem

2.3.1
are now satisfied, see
[

, Thm. 4.10]
. The hom-objects

are the universal measuring comodules, first introduced in
[
Bat00
]
for vector spaces.

Theorem 2.3.5

(Sweedler theory for (co)modules)
.

Suppose
\mathcal{V}
is a locally presentable, symmetric monoidal closed category. The global category of modules
\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{V}}
is tensored and cotensored enriched in the symmetric monoidal closed global category of comodules
\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}
.

We now turn to an enrichment of the fibration of modules over monoids in the opfibration of comodules over comonoids in a monoidal
category, which will later be generalized for (co)monads and (co)modules in double categories. For that purpose, we recall some
relevant concepts and results.

Definition 2.3.6
.

(
[
Shu08
]
)
Let
\mathcal{V}
,
\mathcal{W}
be monoidal categories. A fibration
T\colon\mathcal{V}\to\mathcal{W}
is
monoidal
if

T
is a strict monoidal functor and the tensor product
\otimes_{\mathcal{V}}
preserves cartesian liftings.
It is
braided
or
symmetric
monoidal when it is a braided strict monoidal functor between braided or symmetric monoidal
categories. Dually, there is the notion of a (braided or symmetric)
monoidal opfibration
.

Example 2.3.7
.

The fibration
\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V})
and opfibration
\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathsf{Comon}(\mathcal{V})
as in
6
are both monoidal when

\mathcal{V}
is braided monoidal, since indeed the monoidal structure is strictly preserved,
and it can be
verified that the tensor product preserves (co)cartesian liftings (
[
HLFV17b
, Prop. 4.5]
).

Notice that whereas the global categories
\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{V}}
and
\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}
are monoidal, their fibres
\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{V}}(A)
and
\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}(C)
for a
fixed (co)monoid are not monoidal – since for two
A
-modules
M
and
N
,
M\otimes N
is naturally just an
A\otimes A
-module. This phenomenon
is further discussed in
[
MV20
, § 5.7]
.

We next recall the definition of a fibration enriched in a monoidal fibration, see
[
Vas18
, Def. 3.8]
. If
\mathcal{A}
is a

\mathcal{V}
-enriched category, we denote by
\mathcal{A}(\textrm{-},\textrm{-})
the enriching
hom-object functor, see e.g.
[
Kel05
, § 1.6]
.

Definition 2.3.8
.

A fibration
P\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{X}
is
enriched
in a monoidal fibration
T\colon\mathcal{V}\to\mathcal{W}
when

•

\mathcal{A}
is enriched in
\mathcal{V}
,
\mathcal{X}
is enriched in
\mathcal{W}
and the following commutes

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{V}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{W}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}(-,-)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P^{\mathrm{op}}\times P}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{X}(-,-)}

•

composition and identities of the enrichments are compatible, in that

TM^{\mathcal{A}}_{A,B,C}=M^{\mathcal{X}}_{PA,PB,PC}\;\textrm{ and }\;Tj^{\mathcal{A}}_{A}=j^{\mathcal{X}}_{PA}.

Dually, we have the notion of an enriched opfibration, as well as the following mixed version.

Definition 2.3.9
.

If
T\colon\mathcal{V}\to\mathcal{W}
is a monoidal opfibration, a fibration
P\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{X}
is enriched in the opfibration
T
if the opfibration

P^{\mathrm{op}}
is
T
-enriched.

Remark 2.3.10
.

Notice that for the opfibration
P^{\mathrm{op}}
to be enriched in
T
, the condition “braided” or “symmetric” for the monoidal opfibration
T
(as was
the case in the original reference
[
Vas18
]
) is not really necessary and thus here dropped. What is gained under those
extra assumptions is that the
\mathcal{V}
-enrichment of
\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{op}}
implies that
(\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{op}})^{\mathrm{op}}\cong\mathcal{A}
(or equal in the case of symmetry)
is also
\mathcal{V}
-enriched, and similarly the
\mathcal{W}
-enrichment
\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{op}}
implies that of
\mathcal{X}
. This is of course what happens in the
examples of interest, and as a result motivated the original definition.

Leading to an action-induced enrichment result similar to
Theorem

2.3.1
, below a pseudomonoid acts on a pseudomodule in the
cartesian monoidal 2-category of fibrations,
[
Vas18
, Def. 3.3]
.

Definition 2.3.11
.

A monoidal fibration
T\colon\mathcal{V}\to\mathcal{W}

acts
on a fibration
P\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{X}
when there exists a fibred 1-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{W}\times\mathcal{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces*}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T\times P}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\diamond}

where
*,\diamond
are ordinary actions, such that the action constraints are compatible in that

P\chi^{\mathcal{A}}_{XYA}=\chi^{\mathcal{X}}_{(TX)(TY)(PA)},\quad P\nu^{\mathcal{A}}_{A}=\nu^{\mathcal{X}}_{PA}

for all
X,Y\in\mathcal{V}
and
A\in\mathcal{A}
. Dually, a monoidal opfibration
acts
on an opfibration.

Example 2.3.12
.

If
\mathcal{V}
is a braided monoidal closed category, the monoidal fibration
\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathsf{Comon}(\mathcal{V})^{\mathrm{op}}
acts on the fibration
\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V})
via the fibred 1-cell
8
, where both instances of the internal hom are actions and the required compatibilities hold.

In
[
Vas18
, Thm. 3.11]
, it was proved that if
T\colon\mathcal{V}\to\mathcal{W}
is a monoidal fibration which acts on a fibration

P\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{X}
with a parameterized adjoint
(R,S)\colon P^{\mathrm{op}}\times P\to T
in
\mathsf{Cat}^{\mathbf{2}}
, then we can enrich the fibration
P
in
the monoidal fibration
T
. The parameterized adjunction condition, see
[
Vas18
, Thm. 3.4]
, means that there are adjunctions

\textrm{-}*A\dashv R(A,\textrm{-})
and
\textrm{-}\diamond X\dashv S(X,\textrm{-})
such that

(14)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{V}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{W}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textrm{-}*A}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R(A,\textrm{-})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textrm{-}\diamond PA}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S(PA,\textrm{-})}

is a map of adjunctions (what is called ‘transformation of adjoints’ in
[
ML98
, §IV.7]
), namely (co)units are above one another.
We will here use a version of its dual for a monoidal opfibration acting on the opposite of a fibration
due to our subsequent applications. Notice that concerning enriched fibrations, there are no tensored or cotensored versions investigated in the literature yet.

Theorem 2.3.13
.

Suppose that
T\colon\mathcal{V}\to\mathcal{W}
is a
monoidal opfibration that acts on the opposite of a fibration
P\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{X}
via an opfibred 1-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{op}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{op}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{W}\times\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{op}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{op}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pitchfork^{\mathrm{op}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T\times P^{\mathrm{op}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P^{\mathrm{op}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\square^{\mathrm{op}}}

If
(\pitchfork^{\mathrm{op}},\square^{\mathrm{op}})
has a right parameterized adjoint in
\mathsf{Cat}^{\mathbf{2}}
, then the fibration
P
is enriched in the monoidal
opfibration
T
.

Sketch.

By
Definition

2.3.9
we need to show that the opfibration
P^{\mathrm{op}}
is enriched in the monoidal opfibration
T
.
The adjunctions
(\textrm{-}\pitchfork^{\mathrm{op}}A)\dashv R(A,\textrm{-})
and
(\textrm{-}\square^{\mathrm{op}}X)\dashv S(X,\textrm{-})
give rise to an enrichment of
\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{op}}
in
\mathcal{V}
and
of
\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{op}}
in
\mathcal{W}
(as well as of
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{X}
in case
T
is braided, by
Theorem

2.3.1
)
in such a way that
T\circ\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{op}}(\textrm{-},\textrm{-})=\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{op}}(P\textrm{-},P\textrm{-})
by the parameterized adjunction condition.
Finally, the corresponding composition and identities of enriched categories are compatible, because their adjuncts are. Therefore all clauses of
Definition

2.3.8
are satisfied.
∎

As a result, we obtain the following result (see
[
Vas18
, Prop. 4.1]
4
4

4

Symmetry
assumptions from the references are adjusted according to
Remark

2.3.10
; braiding in
\mathcal{V}
is merely required for
\mathsf{Comon}(\mathcal{V})

and
\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}
to be monoidal categories.
), formally describing
1
.

Theorem 2.3.14
.

For a braided monoidal closed and locally presentable
\mathcal{V}
, the fibration
\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathsf{Mon}(\mathcal{V})
is enriched in the monoidal
opfibration
\mathsf{Comod}_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathsf{Comon}(\mathcal{V})
.

3.
Monads and comonads in double categories, revisited

This chapter is mixed, in that it provides some general background on double categories, fibrant and monoidal structures, and recalls
some results about monads and comonads in double categories appearing in
[
Vas19
]
. However, it goes much further: the notion of a
monoidal closed double category is settled, the notion of a locally presentable double category is introduced, and certain parts of the
development in loc. cit. are much simplified by abstracting some results from the double category
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
to a general double category
\mathbb{D}
.
Its end result,
Theorem

3.4.12
, generalizes Sweedler theory for (co)algebras (
Theorem

2.3.2
) from monoidal categories to double categories.

3.1.
Double categories

We recall some basic material from the theory of double categories, following references like
[
GP99
,
Shu08
]
.
Moreover, we introduce
parallel limits
and
colimits
in double categories (
Definition

3.1.9
) and study some equivalent formulations in terms of
horizontal composition in fibrant double categories.

Definition 3.1.1
.

A
(pseudo) double category

\mathbb{D}

consists of a category of objects
\mathbb{D}_{0}
and
a category of arrows
\mathbb{D}_{1}
, with identity, source and target, composition structure
functors

\mathbf{1}\colon\mathbb{D}_{0}\to\mathbb{D}_{1},\quad\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\colon\mathbb{D}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathbb{D}_{0},\quad\odot\colon\mathbb{D}_{1}{\times_{\mathbb{D}_{0}}}\mathbb{D}_{1}\to\mathbb{D}_{1}

such that

\mathfrak{s}(1_{X})
=
\mathfrak{t}(1_{X})
=
X,\;\mathfrak{s}(M\odot N)
=
\mathfrak{s}(N),\;\mathfrak{t}(M\odot N)
=
\mathfrak{t}(M)

for all
X\in\mathrm{ob}\mathbb{D}_{0}
and
M,N\in\mathrm{ob}\mathbb{D}_{1}
,
equipped with natural isomorphisms

a\colon(M\odot N)\odot P\xrightarrow{\raisebox{-3.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{$\sim$}}M\odot(N\odot P)
,
\ell\colon 1_{\mathfrak{s}(M)}\odot M\xrightarrow{\raisebox{-3.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{$\sim$}}M
,
r\colon M\odot 1_{\mathfrak{t}(M)}\xrightarrow{\raisebox{-3.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{$\sim$}}M

in
\mathbb{D}_{1}
such that

\mathfrak{t}(a),\mathfrak{s}(a),\mathfrak{t}(\ell),\mathfrak{s}(\ell),\mathfrak{t}(r),\mathfrak{s}(r)
are all
identities, and satisfying the usual coherence conditions.

Well-known examples of double categories include
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{pan}(\mathcal{C})
for a category with pullbacks
\mathcal{C}
whose horizontal 1-cells are spans,

\mathbb{R}\mathsf{el}(\mathcal{C})
for a regular category
\mathcal{C}
whose horizontal 1-cells are relations,
\mathbb{B}\mathsf{Mod}
whose horizontal 1-cells are ring
bimodules, and
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}
whose horizontal 1-cells are
\mathcal{V}
-profunctors between
\mathcal{V}
-categories. The latter’s ‘discrete’ version, the double
category of enriched matrices, is the central example of interest to us later; we elaborate below.

Example 3.1.2
.

\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}

or
generalized in

Definition 3.1.3
.

For
\mathbb{D}
and
\mathbb{E}
double categories, a
(pseudo) double functor

F\colon\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{E}

consists of functors
F_{0}:\mathbb{D}_{0}\to\mathbb{E}_{0}
and
F_{1}:\mathbb{D}_{1}\to\mathbb{E}_{1}
such that
\mathfrak{s}\circ F_{1}=F_{0}\circ\mathfrak{s}

and
\mathfrak{t}\circ F_{1}=F_{0}\circ\mathfrak{t}
, and natural transformations
\phi
,
\phi_{0}

with components globular isomorphisms

F_{1}M\odot F_{1}N\xrightarrow{\raisebox{-3.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{$\sim$}}F_{1}(M\odot N)\textrm{ and }1_{F_{0}X}\xrightarrow{\raisebox{-3.0pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{$\sim$}}F_{1}(1_{X})

which satisfy coherence axioms. If these isomorphisms are non-invertible in
that or the reverse direction, we have the notion of a
lax
or
oplax
double functor.

The following lemma recalls some properties of companions and conjoints; proofs can be found in
[
GP04
,
HS19
]
.

Lemma 3.1.5
.

Suppose
f\colon X\to Y
is a vertical morphism in a fibrant double category
\mathbb{D}
.

(3.1.5(i))

Companions and conjoints of
f
are unique up to (unique) globular isomorphism.

(3.1.5(ii))

If
f
is an isomorphism, its structure 2-morphisms
p_{1},p_{2},q_{1},q_{2}
are invertible.

(3.1.5(iii))

There is an adjunction
\widehat{f}\dashv\widecheck{f}
in the horizontal bicategory
\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})
. It becomes an adjoint equivalence when
f

is an isomorphism.

(3.1.5(iv))

For two composable vertical 1-cells,
\widehat{g}\odot\widehat{f}
is a companion and
\widecheck{f}\odot\widecheck{g}
is a conjoint of
gf
.

(3.1.5(v))

If
F\colon\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{E}
is a double functor,
F(\widehat{f})
is a companion and
F(\widecheck{f})
is a conjoint of
Ff
.

The following observations are useful in what comes next, but also later in
Section

4.1
.

Proposition 3.1.8
.

Suppose
\mathbb{D}
is a fibrant double category. Then
\mathfrak{s}
and
\mathfrak{t}
are bifibrations
\mathbb{D}_{1}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
, that restrict to bifibrations

\mathfrak{s}\colon\mathbb{D}^{Y}_{1}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
and
\mathfrak{t}\colon^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
for any object
X,Y
.

Proof.

The source and target functors are separately both bifibrations, formed as

(20)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{0}\times\mathbb{D}_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\rangle}
17
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{2}}

since (op)fibrations compose and projections are (op)fibrations in a straightforward way, see e.g.
[
Bor94
, Prop. 8.1.12&13]
.
In more detail, the reindexing functors of
\mathbb{D}_{1}\xrightarrow{\mathfrak{s}}\mathbb{D}_{0}
for some
f\colon X\to Y
are

{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}\xleftarrow{\textrm{-}\odot\widehat{f}}{}^{Y}\mathbb{D}_{1}
for the fibration and
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}\xrightarrow{\textrm{-}\odot\widecheck{f}}{}^{Y}\mathbb{D}_{1}
for the opfibration
structure, where of course
(\textrm{-}\odot\widecheck{f})\dashv(\textrm{-}\odot\widehat{f})
. Similarly, the reindexing functors of the bifibration

\mathbb{D}_{1}\xrightarrow{\mathfrak{t}}\mathbb{D}_{0}
for
g\colon Z\to W
are

(21)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}^{Z}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}^{W}_{1}.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{g}\odot\textrm{-}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bot}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widecheck{g}\odot\textrm{-}}

Furthermore, both functors restrict to sub-bifibrations.
For example,
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}
is closed under
\mathfrak{t}
-cocartesian lifts inside
\mathbb{D}_{1}
,
since
\widehat{g}\odot M
has the same domain as
M
and the lift is identity on the left. Notice that the fiber above any
Z\in\mathbb{D}_{0}
is

{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}=\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})(X,Z)
, and similarly for
\mathfrak{s}
.
∎

In the present work we will also need to consider (co)limits in various categories arising in the setting of double categories, and so it is
pertinent to introduce the following definition, of essentially a graph internal in the category of
\mathcal{I}
-(co)complete categories and

\mathcal{I}
-(co)limit preserving functors.

Definition 3.1.9
.

Let
\mathbb{D}
be a double category and
\mathcal{I}
is any small category. We shall say that
\mathbb{D}
has
parallel

\mathcal{I}
-(co)limits
if the categories
\mathbb{D}_{0}
,
\mathbb{D}_{1}
both have
\mathcal{I}
-(co)limits and the functors
\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\colon\mathbb{D}_{1}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}

preserve them. If
\mathbb{D}
has parallel
\mathcal{I}
-(co)limits for any small
\mathcal{I}
, then we say that it is
parallel
(co)complete
.

Regarding terminology, ‘parallel’ indicates that this is not a general notion of double-categorical (co)limit e.g. in the sense of

[
GP99
]
, but a more specific one concerning the categories
\mathbb{D}_{1}
and
\mathbb{D}_{0}
. In particular, the term was adopted
from the special case of parallel (co)products appearing in
[
Pat24
]
(mentioned in a talk by Bob Paré in 2009).

Proposition 3.1.10
.

The double category
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
has parallel coproducts.
If, furthermore,
\mathcal{V}
has all colimits and they are preserved by
\otimes
in each variable, then
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
has all parallel colimits.

.
It can be verified that the following 2-morphism is the coequalizer of
\phi,\psi
in
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{1}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Q}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Q^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\omega}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}

where
C
and
\omega
are defined as follows: for each
u\in Q,u^{\prime}\in Q^{\prime}
, form the coequalizer in
\mathcal{V}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sum\limits_{\begin{subarray}{c}qf(x)=u\\
q^{\prime}f^{\prime}(x^{\prime})=u^{\prime}\end{subarray}}A(x^{\prime},x)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sum\limits_{\begin{subarray}{c}q(y)=u\\
q^{\prime}(y^{\prime})=u^{\prime}\end{subarray}}B(y^{\prime},y)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C(u^{\prime},u)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sum\phi_{x,x^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sum\psi_{x,x^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\omega(u,u^{\prime})}

and for any
y\in Y,y^{\prime}\in Y^{\prime}
,
\omega_{y,y^{\prime}}\colon B(y^{\prime},y)\to C(q^{\prime}(y^{\prime}),q(y))
is the following composite in
\mathcal{V}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B(y^{\prime},y)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sum\limits_{\begin{subarray}{c}q(z)=q(y)\\
q^{\prime}(z^{\prime})=q^{\prime}(y^{\prime})\end{subarray}}B(z^{\prime},z)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C(q^{\prime}(y^{\prime}),q(y)).}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\omega(q(y),q^{\prime}(y^{\prime}))}

∎

The level of generality of
Definition

3.1.9
is enough for certain categories of interest to
us, like (co)monads and (co)modules in double categories, to inherit (co)limits – see
Propositions

3.3.6
and
4.1.15
.
Those in fact depend on the following result.

Proposition 3.1.11
.

Let
\mathbb{D}
be a fibrant double category which has parallel
\mathcal{I}
-(co)limits, for some small category
\mathcal{I}
. Then
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
has

\mathcal{I}
-(co)limits and the inclusion
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}\to\mathbb{D}_{1}
preserves them.

Proof.

Consider a diagram
D\colon\mathcal{I}\to\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
whose colimit cocone in
\mathbb{D}_{1}
is

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{i}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{i}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Di}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{i}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\phi_{i}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g_{i}}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}

Since
\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}
preserve colimits, both
f_{i}
and
g_{i}

are colimiting cocones in
\mathbb{D}_{0}
, however of the same diagram in
\mathbb{D}_{0}
since the original
D
lies in
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
. Hence there is
an isomorphism
h\colon Y\cong X
such that
hg_{i}=f_{i}
for all
i\in\mathcal{I}
. This allows us to post-compose the the initial colimit
\phi_{i}
by the
following isomorphism in
\mathbb{D}_{1}

(22)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\cong}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1_{Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow p_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{h}}

where
p_{2}
is invertible since
h
is, by Lemma
3.1.5(ii)
. Hence the new colimiting cocone lies wholly in

\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
, and has the required universal
property.
∎

Remark 3.1.12
.

We here provide a high-level argument for the above result, that will be used in analogous ways in later results as well.
As seen in
16
,
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
is a pullback along
\langle\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\rangle
which in the setting of a fibrant
double category is a fibration
17
. By a standard result (see e.g.
[
JS93b
]
), since every Grothendieck fibration is an isofibration,
the (strict) pullback is equivalent to a
pseudopullback
. Since (co)complete categories with
(co)continuous functors can both be expressed as 2-categories of algebras and pseudo-morphisms
T
-
\mathsf{Alg}
for a 2-monad on
\mathsf{Cat}
,
they have all pseudolimits by the well-known
[
BKP89
, Thm. 2.6]
.
In particular, since
\langle\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\rangle
is (co)continuous under these assumptions, and so is the diagonal
\Delta
, their (pseudo)pullback

\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
is a (co)complete category.

The following result connects the existence of parallel (co)limits in a fibrant double category, to the existence of (co)limits to the various
fixed domain/codomain subcategories of
\mathbb{D}_{1}
, as well as the hom-categories of the horizontal bicategory
\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})
, in a natural way.

Proposition 3.1.13
.

Suppose
\mathbb{D}
is a fibrant double category such that
\mathbb{D}_{0}
is complete. The following are equivalent:

(3.1.13(i))

\mathbb{D}
is parallel complete;

(3.1.13(ii))

The fibrations
\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\colon\mathbb{D}_{1}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
have all fibred limits.

Namely,
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}
and
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}
are complete categories for any
X,Z\in\mathbb{D}_{0}
, and
\textrm{-}\odot\widehat{f}\colon^{Y}\mathbb{D}_{1}\to{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}
and
\widecheck{g}\odot\textrm{-}\colon\mathbb{D}_{1}^{W}\to\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}
are continuous functors for any
f\colon X\to Y
and
g\colon Z\to W
;

(3.1.13(iii))

\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})(X,Z)
is a complete category for any
X,Z\in\mathbb{D}_{0}
, and

\textrm{-}\odot\widehat{f}\colon\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})(Y,Z)\to\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})(X,Z)
and
\widecheck{g}\odot\textrm{-}\colon\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})(X,W)\to\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})(X,Z)
are continuous
functors.

Dually, if
\mathbb{D}_{0}
is cocomplete, the following are equivalent:

(3.1.13(i))

\mathbb{D}
is parallel cocomplete;

(3.1.13(ii))

The opfibrations
\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\colon\mathbb{D}_{1}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
have all opfibred colimits.

Namely,
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}
and
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}
are cocomplete for any
X,Z\in\mathbb{D}_{0}
, and

\textrm{-}\odot\widecheck{f}\colon{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}\to{}^{Y}\mathbb{D}_{1}
and
\widehat{g}\odot\textrm{-}\colon\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}\to\mathbb{D}_{1}^{W}
are cocontinuous functors for any
f\colon X\to Y
and

g\colon Z\to W
;

(3.1.13(iii))

\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})(X,Z)={}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}
is a cocomplete category for any
X,Z\in\mathbb{D}_{0}
, and

\textrm{-}\odot\widecheck{f}\colon{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}\to{}^{Y}\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}
and
\widehat{g}\odot\textrm{-}\colon{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}\to{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}^{W}
are cocontinuous
functors.

Proof.

We will verify the version for limits; the version for colimits is dual.

(i)\Leftrightarrow(ii)
This follows essentially from
Proposition

2.2.2
. In more detail, if
\mathbb{D}_{1}
is complete and
\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}
are continuous functors as per

Definition

3.1.9
, the fibration
\mathfrak{s}
of
Proposition

3.1.8
has all fibred limits, which means that all fibers
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}
have limits
and the reindexing functors
\textrm{-}\odot\widehat{f}\colon^{Y}\mathbb{D}_{1}\to{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}
for any
f\colon X\to Y
are continuous. Similarly for the fibration
\mathfrak{t}
.

Conversely, if all
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}
have limits and all appropriate
\textrm{-}\odot\widehat{f}
preserve them, this means that the fibration
\mathfrak{s}
is complete. Since its base category
\mathbb{D}_{0}
is also complete, it follows from
Proposition

2.2.2
that
\mathbb{D}_{1}
has all limits and
\mathfrak{s}
preserves them. Similarly,
\mathfrak{t}
is also continuous hence
\mathbb{D}
is parallel complete.

(ii)\Rightarrow(iii)

It can be verified that the restricted fibration

\mathfrak{s}\colon\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}

from
Proposition

3.1.8
is continuous. Indeed,
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}
is a fiber of the target fibration, which has all fibred limits, hence it is complete. Furthermore, connected limits
are preserved under the inclusion
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{D}_{1}
by
Corollary

2.2.3
. Given the equivalence of (1) and (2), we know that
\mathfrak{s}
preserves all limits, hence so does the composite
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{D}_{1}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
. For discrete limits, by their general construction
in
9
and the form of the reindexing functors of
\mathfrak{t}

21
namely
\Delta^{*}=\widecheck{\Delta}\odot\textrm{-}
, it is the case that the source of the limit horizontal 1-cell
remains unchanged.

Thus, by
Proposition

2.2.2
the fibers
\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})(X,Z)
of the continuous
\mathfrak{s}\colon\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
are also complete
and the restricted reindexing functors
\textrm{-}\odot\widecheck{f}
preserve all limits. In a similar fashion, the restricted fibration
\mathfrak{t}\colon{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
can be seen to preserve all
limits, so also the restricted
\widehat{g}\odot\textrm{-}
on the horizontal bicategory hom-categories also preserve all limits.

(iii)\Rightarrow(ii)
Since every
\textrm{-}\odot\widehat{f}\colon\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})(Y,Z)\to\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})(X,Z)
is continuous and
\mathbb{D}_{0}
is complete, the
restricted
fibration
\mathfrak{s}\colon\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
from
Proposition

3.1.8
is complete for all objects
Z
, which in particular means that all

\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}
are complete. Now we can form the following commutative triangle

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{1}^{W}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{0}.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widecheck{g}\odot\textrm{-}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{s}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{s}}

Since
(\widehat{g}\odot\textrm{-})\dashv(\widecheck{g}\odot\textrm{-})
is such that the counit is
\mathfrak{s}
-vertical, they form an adjunction in
\mathsf{Cat}/\mathbb{D}_{0}
and so
by a standard argument where right adjoints in the slice category are cartesian (see e.g.
[
Win90
, Lem. 4.5]
), the top arrow preserves cartesian liftings. As a result, by
Proposition

2.2.4

in the special case that the functor between the bases is the identity, the fact that the fiberwise

\widecheck{g}\odot\textrm{-}\colon\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})(X,W)\to\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})(X,Z)
are continuous by assumption implies that the “global” functor

\widecheck{g}\odot\textrm{-}\colon\mathbb{D}_{1}^{W}\to\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}
is continuous.

In an analogous way, now starting from the fact that
\widecheck{g}\odot\textrm{-}\colon\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})(X,W)\to\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})(X,Z)
is continuous and
\mathbb{D}_{0}
is
complete, we can deduce that the restricted fibration
\mathfrak{t}\colon{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
from
Proposition

3.1.8
is complete thus ensuring that
each
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}
is complete, which can then be used to form a fibred functor

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}^{Y}\mathbb{D}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textrm{-}\odot\widehat{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{t}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{t}}

since
\textrm{-}\odot\widehat{f}
is again a right adjoint over
\mathbb{D}_{0}
. The fiberwise continuous restrictions of
\textrm{-}\odot\widehat{f}
from the assumptions then
make the functor between the total categories continuous.
∎

Remark 3.1.14
.

One extra advantage of the above equivalent formulations of
Proposition

3.1.13
in the fibrant setting is that they connect the notion
of a parallel cocomplete double category to the more standard one of a “locally cocomplete bicategory”, see e.g.
[
BCSW83
]
. In more
detail, if a fibrant
double category
\mathbb{D}
is such that
\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})
is locally cocomplete, namely all hom-categories are cocomplete and all functors of the form

M\odot\textrm{-}\odot N
preserve colimits, condition (3) above is clearly verified when
\mathbb{D}
is also “vertically” cocomplete. This is
important because checking that a horizontal bicategory of a double category is locally cocomplete in the usual sense could be much easier. For
example, (co)limits in the hom-categories
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Mat}(X,Y)=[Y\times X,\mathcal{V}]
are computed pointwise, and horizontal composition preserves colimits by
usual assumptions on the monoidal structure of
\mathcal{V}
, hence we recover that
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Mat}
is parallel cocomplete –
Proposition

3.1.10
.

3.2.
Monoidal closed double categories

We now move to the context of monoidal double categories, see e.g.
[
HS19
, Def. 2.10]
for a detailed description. We then describe in detail a monoidal closed double structure pertinent to our purposes.

Definition 3.2.1
.

A
monoidal double category
is a double category
\mathbb{D}
such that
(\mathbb{D}_{0},\otimes_{0},I)
and

(\mathbb{D}_{1},\otimes_{1},1_{I})
are monoidal categories,
\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}
are strict monoidal functors, and there exist globular isomorphisms

(23)

(M\otimes_{1}N)\odot(M^{\prime}\otimes_{1}N^{\prime})\cong(M\odot M^{\prime})\otimes_{1}(N\odot N^{\prime}),\quad 1_{(X\otimes_{0}Y)}\cong 1_{X}\otimes_{1}1_{Y}

subject to coherence conditions.

The natural isomorphisms come from the fact that there are pseudo double functors
\otimes\colon\mathbb{D}\times\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{D}
and

I\colon\mathbf{1}\to\mathbb{D}
expressing that a monoidal double category
is a pseudomonoid in a suitable cartesian 2-category of double categories.
A
braided
or
symmetric
monoidal double category
\mathbb{D}
is one for which
\mathbb{D}_{0}
,
\mathbb{D}_{1}
are
braided or symmetric, and
\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}
are strict braided monoidal, subject to two more axioms expressing compatibility of the braiding with the
structure isomorphisms.

Example 3.2.2
.

The double category
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
from
Example

3.1.2
is monoidal when
\mathcal{V}
is moreover braided. The vertical category is the cartesian

(\mathbf{Set},\times,\{*\})
and
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{1}
is monoidal via

\otimes_{1}\colon\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{1}\times\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{1}\xrightarrow{\phantom{AAAAAAA}}\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{1}\phantom{AAAAA}

The isomorphisms
23
come down to the tensor product in
\mathcal{V}
being braided and commuting with coproducts, see

.

Notice that
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
is not a braided monoidal double category under these assumptions, because the braiding fails to become a transformation of double categories. However,
if the braiding of
\mathcal{V}
is a symmetry, that extra axiom is satisfied and
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
becomes a symmetric monoidal double category.

represented by
X\times X^{\prime}\xleftarrow{r_{0}\times r_{0}^{{}^{\prime}}}R\times R^{\prime}\xrightarrow{r_{1}\times r_{1}^{{}^{\prime}}}Y\times Y^{\prime}
.
The globular isomorphisms required are the equalities
(S\times S^{\prime})(R\times R^{\prime})=(SR)\times(S^{\prime}R^{\prime})
and
\Delta_{X\times Y}=\Delta_{X}\times\Delta_{Y}
, which boil down to the stability of regular epimorphisms under finite products in the regular category
\mathcal{C}
.
Notice that the bicategory
\mathsf{Rel}(\mathcal{C})
does not have products without additional assumptions on
\mathcal{C}
.

In
[
Vas19
, § 3.3]
, a notion of a ‘locally closed’ monoidal double category was introduced, that renders both ordinary categories
\mathbb{D}_{0}

and
\mathbb{D}_{1}
monoidal closed. We here revisit this notion, moreover dropping the term ‘locally’, by first taking a closer look to general adjoints for double categories, see

[
GP04
, §3.2]
.

Definition 3.2.4
.

An
oplax/lax
adjunction
F\dashv R
between double categories consists of

•

an oplax double functor
(F,\phi,\phi_{0})\colon\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{E}

•

a lax double functor
(R,\rho,\rho_{0})\colon\mathbb{E}\to\mathbb{D}

•

two ordinary adjunctions
F_{0}\dashv R_{0}
and
F_{1}\dashv R_{1}
that respect the source and target – equivalently
(\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{s})
and

(\mathfrak{t},\mathfrak{t})
are maps of adjunctions

•

the counits are compatible with the structure maps

5

GP04
]

FR
and
RF
are
neither lax nor oplax double functors.

However, as mentioned also in
[
GP04
, Remark 3.3a]
, this and condition
24
in fact specify the
structure cells of the
functors involved in terms of one another. For example,
24
express
(\rho,\rho_{0})
of
G
in terms of

(\phi,\phi_{0})
of
F
by providing their transposes under the adjunction
F_{1}\dashv G_{1}
.
One can verify, using naturality of the
structure maps and (co)units, that just one of
24
or
25
is enough to imply the other, therefore can be safely omitted
from the definition.

This situation is reminiscent of the well-known
doctrinal adjunction

for adjoints between monoidal categories, where oplax monoidal structures on
the left adjoint bijectively correspond to lax monoidal structures on the right adjoint. Following the above discussion, the theorem below gives
simple conditions under which an oplax double functor has a lax double right adjoint.

Theorem 3.2.6
.

Suppose
F\colon\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{E}
is an oplax double functor. If

•

F_{0}
and
F_{1}
have ordinary right adjoints
R_{0}
and
R_{1}
respectively; and

•

the source and target functors form maps of adjunctions depicted in

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{E}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{E}_{0},}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{s}/\mathfrak{t}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bot}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{s}/\mathfrak{t}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bot}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R_{0}}

then
(R_{0},R_{1})
forms a lax double functor, which is part of an oplax/lax adjunction
F\dashv R
.

Proof.

We define the required lax structure 2-cells
\rho_{M,N}\colon RN\odot RM\to R(N\odot M)
and
\rho_{0}\colon 1_{RY}\to R(1_{Y})
for the pair
(R_{0},R_{1})
by giving their adjuncts precisely as in
24
. For this data to form a lax double functor structure as in
Definition

3.1.3
, we already know that
R_{0},R_{1}
strictly commute with the source and
target functors from the second clause above, and also naturality of
\rho,\rho_{0}
follows from naturality of
\phi,\phi_{0}
and
\varepsilon
.
Finally, the coherence axioms can be verified, performing the relevant calculations ‘under the adjunction’. As a sample check, we verify that
for composable horizontal 1-cells
M,N,U
, we have an equality of globular 2-cells
\rho_{N\circ M,U}(\mathrm{id}_{RU}\circ\rho_{M,N})=\rho_{M,U\circ N}(\rho_{N,U}\circ\mathrm{id}_{RM})
.
Translating under the adjunction
F_{1}\dashv G_{1}
, suppressing associativity for horizontal composition, we have the following steps

. The other two unit axioms can be proved

To conclude the proof, notice that all clauses of
Definition

3.2.4
hold by default.
∎

Let us remark that the above result could be viewed as a special case of the more general
[
Par15
, Thm. 4.8]
, where the right
adjoints

G_{0}
and
G_{1}
are required to commute with the source and target only up to isomorphism via the corresponding mates, hence in particular cannot
form a double functor right away.
However, a direct calculation as in the above proof (which does not include the ‘wobbly functors’ of
loc. cit.
) is clearer for our setting.

Moving on towards our goal, namely specifying a certain type of double adjoint for the tensor product of a monoidal double category, we now discuss

parameterized
double adjunctions. Recall the original concept of an ordinary ‘adjunction with a parameter’ found e.g. in
[
ML98
, §IV.7]
.

Theorem 3.2.7
.

Suppose that
F\colon\mathbb{A}\times\mathbb{B}\to\mathbb{C}
is an oplax double functor. If

(3.2.7(i))

F_{0}
and
F_{1}
have ordinary parameterized adjoints
R_{0}
and
R_{1}
respectively; and

(3.2.7(ii))

the source and target functors are maps of adjunctions as follows

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{A}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{A}_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{1}(\textrm{-},B)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{s}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bot}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{s}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R_{1}(B,\textrm{-})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{0}(\textrm{-},{\mathfrak{s}}B)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bot}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R_{0}({\mathfrak{s}}B,\textrm{-})}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{A}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{A}_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{0},}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{1}(\textrm{-},B)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{t}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bot}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{t}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R_{1}(B,\textrm{-})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{0}(\textrm{-},{\mathfrak{t}}B)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bot}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R_{0}({\mathfrak{t}}B,\textrm{-})}

then
(R_{0},R_{1})\colon\mathbb{B}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{A}
forms a lax double functor, called the
parameterized double adjoint
of
F
.

Proof.

By definition of a double functor,
(F_{0},F_{1})
is a morphism of two variables in
\mathsf{Cat}^{\mathbf{2}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{A}_{1}\times\mathbb{B}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{A}_{0}\times\mathbb{B}_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{C}_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{s}\times\mathfrak{s}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{s}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{0}}

and similarly a morphism from
\mathfrak{t}\times\mathfrak{t}
to
\mathfrak{t}
. As also briefly recalled in
Section

2.3
,

[
Vas18
, Thm. 3.4]
ensures that under these assumptions, the pair of ordinary parameterized adjoints
(R_{0},R_{1})
induced already
by
(i)
is such that the following square commutes

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{B}^{\mathrm{op}}_{1}\times\mathbb{C}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{A}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{B}^{\mathrm{op}}_{0}\times\mathbb{C}_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{A}_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{s}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathfrak{s}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{s}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R_{0}}

and similarly for
\mathfrak{t}
. Finally, the oplax double structure maps
(\rho,\rho_{0})
for
F
uniquely induce structure maps
(\phi,\phi_{0})
that make

(R_{0},R_{1})
into a lax double functor in
a completely analogous way to the proof of
Theorem

3.2.6
, but now in the parameterized setting. In more detail, the adjuncts of the required maps, for horizontal
1-cells

As pointed out above, the induced structure maps
(\phi,\phi_{0})
on
R
are the parameterized versions of
24
,
and the proof that they form a lax structure follows the parameterized analogue of the doctrinal adjunction for monoidal categories:
oplax monoidal structures on functors of two variables on the left, bijectively correspond to lax monoidal structures on the right parameterized adjoint of two variables – see

[
Vas14
, Prop. 3.2.3]
for an explicit proof or
[
DS97
, Prop. 2]
for a higher dimensional version.

Finally, notice how in the ordinary setting, a parameterized adjunction is essentially defined via the following formulation, whereas in the double categorical setting it is strictly weaker than the presence of a fully fledged double adjoint.

Corollary 3.2.8
.

For a parameterized oplax/lax double adjunction
F\dashv G
between functors of two variables
F\colon\mathbb{A}\times\mathbb{B}\to\mathbb{C}
and
G\colon\mathbb{B}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{A}
, in particular we obtain oplax/lax double adjunctions
F(\textrm{-},X)\dashv G(X,\textrm{-})
for any
X\in\mathbb{B}
.

Proof.

Checking all clauses of
Definition

3.2.4
for the oplax and lax, respectively, double functors
(F_{0}(\textrm{-},X),F_{1}(\textrm{-},1_{X}))\colon\mathbb{A}\to\mathbb{C}
and
(G_{0}(X,\textrm{-}),G_{1}(1_{X},\textrm{-}))\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{A}
, by default we have two ordinary adjunctions
F_{0}(\textrm{-},X)\dashv G_{0}(X,\textrm{-})
and
F_{1}(\textrm{-},1_{X})\dashv G_{1}(1_{X},\textrm{-})
that respect the source and target. For the second family of adjunctions, notice that
F_{1}\dashv G_{1}
being parameterized adjoints is strictly more general, since the fixed-variable adjunctions exist for arbitrary horizontal 1-cells and not just those of the form
1_{X}
. Finally, it can be shown that the counits are compatibe with the structure maps, using the respective parameterized compatibilities
26
and dinaturality of counits.
∎

We have now laid all necessary groundwork in order to position the notion of a monoidal closed double category in its natural context.

Definition 3.2.9
.

A monoidal double category
(\mathbb{D},\otimes,I)
is
closed
if the pseudo
double functor
\otimes\colon\mathbb{D}\times\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{D}
has a parameterized double adjoint, namely a lax double functor

(27)

H=(H_{0},H_{1})\colon\mathbb{D}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbb{D}\longrightarrow\mathbb{D}

such that:

(1)

\otimes_{0}\dashv H_{0}
and
\otimes_{1}\dashv H_{1}
are parameterized adjunctions, so
\mathbb{D}_{0}
and
\mathbb{D}_{1}
are monoidal closed
categories;

(2)

for every horizontal 1-cell
M\colon X\hbox to38pt{\vbox to9.92pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 18.99997pt\lower-2.46147pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {}{}{}{}{}{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{}{}{{{}}{{}}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{}{{

Also notice that the definition implies that
