are closed functors.

Remark 3.2.10
.

In
[
GP04
, §5.5]
, Grandis and Paré briefly define a
weakly monoidal closed
double category, as one where each oplax double functor
\textrm{-}\otimes X
has a lax right double adjoint. In light of
Corollary

3.2.8
, such a formulation is strictly less general than
Definition

3.2.9
and any monoidal closed double category is in particular a weakly such.

In fact, following terminology introduced by Niefield in the setting of
cartesian closed
double categories
[
Nie24
]
, one could call such a weakly monoidal closed double category an
object-wise
monoidal closed one. That latter work is certainly relevant to the current material and although independently developed, the observation that a parameterized adjunction can equivalently be defined via object-wise adjunctions in the ordinary setting whereas that equivalence breaks in the double categorical setting, is key.

Remark 3.2.11
.

The original definition of a locally closed monoidal double category in
[
Vas19
, § 3.3]
did not explicitly include condition
2

– as well as the parameterized double adjunction framework that backs it up.
However, the said condition is in fact necessary for certain constructions, e.g. the induced monoidal closed structure on the endomorphism category

\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
:
as in
[
Vas19
, Prop. 3.21]
, we restrict the natural isomorphisms
\mathbb{D}_{1}(M\otimes_{1}N,P)\cong\mathbb{D}_{1}(M,H_{1}(N,P))
to endo-1-cells and
endo-2-morphisms. In
particular, the latter statement implies that the conjugate of an endo-2-morphism along the adjunction
\otimes_{1}\dashv H_{1}
is again
an
endo
-2-morphism.

Example 3.2.12
.

The double category
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
from
Example

3.2.2
is monoidal closed, when
\mathcal{V}
is furthermore monoidal closed with products.
The relevant structure was detailed in
[
Vas19
, Cor. 4.4]
but in the current setting requires less checks, since for example the lax double structure of
H

follows from
Theorem

3.2.7
.

To recall the structure, the clauses of

are satisfied as follows.

Example 3.2.13
.

The double category
\mathbb{R}\mathsf{el}(\mathcal{\mathsf{Set}})
is monoidal closed. The vertical part of the required structure comes from the familiar cartesian closure of
\mathsf{Set}
. In addition, for any
f\in A^{X}
and
g\in B^{Y}
define
(f,g)\in S^{R}
to mean that the
implication
(x,y)\in R\rightarrow(f(x),g(y))\in S
holds for all
x\in X
and
y\in Y
, yielding a lax double
functor
\mathbb{R}\mathsf{el}(\mathcal{\mathsf{Set}})^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbb{R}\mathsf{el}(\mathcal{\mathsf{Set}})\to\mathbb{R}\mathsf{el}(\mathcal{\mathsf{Set}})
. For the clauses of
Definition

3.2.9
, we verify that there is a bijection between
2-cells of the following forms

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C\times X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D\times Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T\times R}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B^{Y}}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tilde{f}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tilde{g}}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S^{R}}

i.e. the inclusion of relations
g(T\times R)f^{\circ}\subseteq S
is equivalent to
\tilde{g}T\tilde{f}^{\circ}\subseteq S^{R}
.

Assume the first of these holds and consider any
c\in C
and
d\in D
such that
(c,d)\in T
. We need to show that
(\tilde{f}(c),\tilde{g}(d))\in S^{R}
. So let
x\in X
and
y\in Y
be such that
(x,y)\in R
. Then
((c,x),(d,y))\in T\times R
and hence by assumption we have
(f(c,x),g(d,y))\in S
, as desired.

Conversely, assume that
\tilde{g}T\tilde{f}^{\circ}\subseteq S^{R}
and let
(c,x)\in C\times X
and
(d,y)\in D\times Y
be such that

((c,x),(d,y))\in T\times R
. Then we have
(x,y)\in R
and
(c,d)\in T
. Since
(\tilde{f}(c),\tilde{g}(d))\in S^{R}
by our assumption, we deduce
that
(\tilde{f}(c)(x),\tilde{g}(d)(y))\in S
, i.e. that
(f(c,x),g(d,y))\in S
.

Finally, it is clear from the description of the bijection given above that the counits of the adjunctions
-\times R\dashv(-)^{R}
in
\mathbb{R}\mathsf{el}(\mathcal{\mathsf{Set}})_{1}
have vertical morphisms the corresponding counits in
\mathsf{Set}
. In other words they are of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{X}\times X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B^{Y}\times Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S^{R}\times R}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{ev}_{X,A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\mathrm{ev}_{R,S}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{ev}_{Y,B}}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S}

which gives the second clause of definition
3.2.9
.

3.3.
Monads and comonads

Similarly to monads and comonads in bicategories recalled in
Section

2.1
, we can define such structures in double categories. In fact,
as objects
they coincide with those of the corresponding horizontal bicategory, however the morphisms are more flexible.

comes with appropriate cocomposition and coidentity arrows

\displaystyle\delta_{x,z}\colon C(x,z)\to\sum_{y\in X}{C(x,y)\otimes C(y,z)}

satisfying coassociativity and counitality laws.
Since (co)monad morphisms in
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
are precisely
\mathcal{V}
-(co)functors,
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at})\cong\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Cat}
and

\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at})\cong\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Cocat}
. We note that this illustrates a conceptual advantage of double categories as opposed to bicategories, since we
can equally well describe
\mathcal{V}
-categories as monads in the (horizontal) bicategory
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Mat}
, however, it is then no longer
true that monad morphisms bijectively correspond to
\mathcal{V}
-functors.

of

or

Proposition 3.3.4
.

Suppose

To first ensure that
\delta
– the candidate for comultiplication – is actually a globular morphism, observe that since
\mathfrak{s}
(or

\mathfrak{t}
) preserves colimits, the cocone
(f_{i}\colon X_{i}\to X)_{i\in\mathcal{I}}
is a colimit in the category
\mathbb{D}_{0}
. Then, the above in
particular implies that
uf_{i}=f_{i}
for all
i\in\mathcal{I}
, hence
u=\mathrm{id}_{X}
.

imply the existence of a unique morphism
{}^{v}\epsilon^{v}
in
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
from
C
to the colimit of the
1_{X_{i}}
’s
that satisfy
\epsilon\phi_{i}=(1_{f_{i}})\epsilon_{i}
for all
i\in\mathcal{I}
,
which in particular gives
v=\mathrm{id}_{X}
, i.e.
\epsilon
is globular.

We will now show that
\delta
together with
\epsilon
endow
C
with a comonad structure. Note that, once
this goal has been accomplished, the

Since this holds for all
i\in\mathcal{I}
, by the colimit property in
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
we deduce that
(\epsilon\odot 1)\delta\cong 1
.
Coassociativity is established in an analogous way through calculations providing an equality
(\Delta\odot 1)\Delta\phi_{i}=(1\odot\Delta)\Delta\phi_{i}
.

Finally, one can use similar arguments to show that the uniquely induced morphism
C\Rightarrow B
for a different colimit candidate
B
is in
fact a morphism of comonads, as soon as
B\in\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})
is the vertex of a cocone over the diagram
D
in
\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})
.
∎

Corollary 3.3.7
.

Let
\mathbb{D}
be a fibrant double category. If it is parallel complete, then the fibration
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
has all fibred limits. If
\mathbb{D}

is parallel cocomplete, then the opfibration
\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
has all fibred colimits.

Proof.

In a parallel complete double category (
Definition

3.1.9
), the functors
\mathfrak{s}/\mathfrak{t}\colon\mathbb{D}_{1}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
are continuous.
In a fibrant such double category,
Propositions

3.3.6
and
3.1.11
ensure that limits are preserved through

\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}\to\mathbb{D}_{1}
. Therefore the fibration
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
of
Proposition

3.3.4
(ii) which is the composite of the above functors
has all fibred limits, by
Proposition

2.2.2
. Analogously we verify the case of comonads.

In particular, this means that the reindexing functors
\widecheck{f}\odot\textrm{-}\odot\widehat{f}\colon\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})_{Y}\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})_{X}
preserve all limits,
and the reindexing functors
\widehat{f}\odot\textrm{-}\odot\widecheck{f}\colon\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})_{X}\to\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})_{Y}
preserve all colimits, for any
f\colon X\to Y
.
∎

Similarly to lax or oplax monoidal functors between monoidal categories, double functors preserve monads or comonads accordingly in a
natural way. For a full proof, see
[
Vas19
, Prop. 3.12]
.

Proposition 3.3.8
.

Any lax double functor
F=(F_{0},F_{1})\colon\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{E}
induces an ordinary functor

\mathsf{Mnd}F:\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{E})

between their categories of monads, by restricting

F_{1}
to
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
. Dually, any oplax double functor induces
\mathsf{Cmd}F\colon\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{E})

between the categories of comonoids.

Sketch.

A monad
(A,\mu,\eta)
in
\mathbb{D}
is mapped to the monad
(FA,F(\mu)\phi,F(\eta)\phi_{0})
in
\mathbb{E}
, i.e. vertically composing the mapped
monad structures with the lax double functor structure maps.
∎

becomes a lax monoidal functor between the corresponding monoidal categories, therefore reducing

to the standard

2
, as was the case for bicategories and lax functors.

As a corollary to
Proposition

3.3.8
, we deduce that the double functor
\otimes\colon\mathbb{D}\times\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{D}
for a
monoidal double category induces tensor product functors for (co)monads.

Proposition 3.3.10
.

If
\mathbb{D}
is a (braided/symmetric) monoidal double category, then the categories
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
and
\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})
inherit a
(braided/symmetric) monoidal structure from
\mathbb{D}_{1}
.

Proposition 3.3.11
.

For a (braided/symmetric) monoidal fibrant double category
\mathbb{D}
, the fibration
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
and the opfibration

\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
are (braided/symmetric) monoidal.

Remark 3.3.12
.

As recalled in
Remark

3.3.9
, a double category with a single object
and a single vertical arrow reduces to a monoidal category.
Clearly, since horizontal composition plays the role of the tensor product,
this monoidal category is not expected to be braided.

When the double category is monoidal,
\mathbb{D}_{1}

has two monoidal structures
\odot
and
\otimes
that interact as in
23

and also share their monoidal unit. By an
Eckmann-Hilton type argument, see
[
AM10
, Prop. 6.11]
, it can be verified
that this (one object,one vertical arrow)-case of a monoidal double category
gives rise to a braided monoidal category, according also to the so-called

periodic table

[
BD95
]
for the one-object case of a monoidal
bicategory. In that case,
\odot\cong\otimes
and the categories of (co)monoids
– seen as (co)monads in the trivial case – become monoidal as discussed
earlier.

Notice that when
\otimes
is braided, in its suspended case it
automatically becomes symmetric
[
AM10
, Prop. 6.13]
thus monoids and
comonoids inherit it directly as such.

3.3.8

\mathbb{D}

In the fibrant context, we furthermore know that the legs in the above diagram
are fibrations by
Proposition

3.3.4
. Since
right adjoints in
\mathsf{Cat}^{\mathbf{2}}
preserve cartesian arrows (see

[
Jac99
, Ex. 9.4.4]
), we deduce that
H(M,\textrm{-})
preserves cartesian liftings. Finally, it is verified that its restriction

H(C,\textrm{-})\colon\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
for any comonad
C\colon Z\to Z
also preserves cartesian liftings, essentially because
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
is
closed under liftings in
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
. In more detail, starting with a cartesian lifting on the left, we apply
(H(C,\textrm{-}),H(Z,\textrm{-}))
on the right

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(C,\widecheck{f}\odot B\odot\widehat{f})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widecheck{f}\odot B\odot\widehat{f}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textrm{in }\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widecheck{H(1,f)}\odot H(C,B)\odot\widehat{H(1,f)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(C,B)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textrm{in }\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textrm{in }\mathbb{D}_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(Z,X)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(Z,Y)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textrm{in }\mathbb{D}_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(1,\mathrm{Cart}(f,B))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\exists!k}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cart}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cart}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mapsto}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(1,f)}

and there exists a unique map
k
that makes the above triangle commute in
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
, therefore in particular in
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
.
Now since cartesian liftings of the underlying endoarrows in
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
coincide with those in
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
, by the above discussion

H(1,\mathrm{Cart}(f,B))
is cartesian in
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
above
H(1,f)
therefore there exists a unique isomorphism
u\colon H(C,\widecheck{f}\odot B\odot\widehat{f})\cong\widecheck{H(1,f)}\odot H(C,B)\odot\widehat{H(1,f)}
in
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
that commutes with
\mathrm{Cart}
and
H(1,\mathrm{Cart})
. Although
u
is not
required to be a monad map to begin with, universality forces
k
to be equal to
u
hence an isomorphism of monads, and the proof is complete.

For preservation of liftings by
H
on the first variable, consider the following square

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet})^{\mathrm{op}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{0}^{\mathrm{op}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{H(\textrm{-},N)}^{\mathrm{op}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{s}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bot}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{s}^{\mathrm{op}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(\textrm{-},N)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(\textrm{-},Y)^{\mathrm{op}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bot}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(\textrm{-},Y)}

that commutes on both sides, where such adjunctions arise in any ordinary braided monoidal closed category. This is also a map of adjunctions, since the counit (the usual
double-dual embedding) in
\mathbb{D}_{1}
on the left is defined via its tensor-hom adjunct on the right

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(H(X,Z),Z)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(H(X,Z),Z)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(H(M,N),N)}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(X,Z)\otimes X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(X,Z)\otimes X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{ev}_{X,Z}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(M,N)\otimes M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\mathrm{ev}_{M,N}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{ev}_{X,Z}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N}

hence the source/target of the counit 2-cell on the left is the counit vertical map for
\mathbb{D}_{0}
as per
28
. Thus viewing
the legs as fibrations (since
\mathfrak{s}{=}\mathfrak{t}

are bifibrations), the right adjoint
H(\textrm{-},N)
preserves cartesian liftings. In a similar way to above, we can verify that the restricted functor
between monads
H(\textrm{-},B)\colon\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D}^{\mathrm{op}})=\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
for a fixed monad
B
still preserves cartesian liftings, essentially
because
\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})
and
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
are closed under cocartesian and cartesian liftings respectively in
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
as seen in

Proposition

3.3.4
.
∎

Remark 3.3.14
.

It is the case that for a monoidal closed double category

Example 3.3.15
.

In the case
\mathbb{D}=\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
for a
\mathcal{V}
which is monoidal closed with products, the induced functor
31
between the categories of
(co)monads (
Example

3.3.3
) is

H\colon\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Cocat}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Cat}\longrightarrow\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Cat}

mapping a pair
(C_{X},B_{Y})
of
\mathcal{V}
-cocategory and a
\mathcal{V}
-category to a
\mathcal{V}
-category
H(C,B)_{Y^{X}}
with hom-objects

H(C,B)(s,k)=\prod_{x,x^{\prime}}[C(x,x^{\prime}),B(sx,kx^{\prime})]
, and composition arrows

\prod_{a,a^{\prime}}{[C(a,a^{\prime}),B(sa,ka^{\prime})]}\otimes\prod_{b,b^{\prime}}{[C(b,b^{\prime}),B(kb,tb^{\prime})]}\to\prod_{c,c^{\prime}}{[C(c,c^{\prime}),B(sc,tc^{\prime})]}

defined via their transpose under the tensor-hom adjunction in
\mathcal{V}
, using the (co)composition arrows and the fact that
\otimes
commutes with
sums accordingly, generalizing the convolution product.

3.4.
Locally presentable double categories and enrichment

In Theorems 3.23 and 3.24 of
[
Vas19
]
, the enrichment of monads in comonads as well as the enriched fibration structure is
subject to the extra condition that
H
as well as the pair

(H\colon\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D}),H_{0}\colon\mathbb{D}_{0}^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbb{D}_{0}\to\mathbb{D}_{0})
as in
Proposition

3.3.13
have appropriate adjoints.
Considering whether this is true in a general double context led us to consider a notion of a
locally
presentable
double category, or essentially one on the ‘local’ level of
\mathbb{D}_{0}
and
\mathbb{D}_{1}
, as a
sufficient setting. Although a general investigation of such a topic would go beyond the scope of the current work, given how even on the level of
2-categories relevant research is still ongoing (see e.g.
[
DL23
,
Bou21
]
), we here introduce such a notion which in the same spirit
as
Definition

3.2.9
serves for our purposes. By doing so, we manage to obtain the relevant results in a more general double categorical
context than
[
Vas19
]
, as exhibited in
Theorem

3.4.12
.

Recall that
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}
and
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{X}
are the the fixed-domain and fixed-codomain subcategories of
\mathbb{D}_{1}
as defined in the beginning of
Section

3.1
.

\mathbb{D}

\lxSVG@closescope {{

, the functors
-\odot M\colon^{Y}\mathbb{D}_{1}\to{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}
and
M\odot-\colon\mathbb{D}_{1}^{X}\to\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Y}
are accessible.

\mathbb{D}
will be called
locally presentable
if it is locally
\lambda
-presentable for some regular cardinal
\lambda
.

As a direct implication of the above definition, we obtain the following.

Corollary 3.4.2
.

A locally presentable double category
\mathbb{D}
is parallel complete and cocomplete. Moreover,
\mathfrak{s}
and
\mathfrak{t}
both have all fibred limits and opfibred colimits.

Proof.

Definition

3.1.9
is straight away satisfied by the clauses of the locally presentable double category definition. Moreover, the source and
target fibrations of
Proposition

3.1.8
satisfy the clauses of
Proposition

2.2.2
.
∎

Perhaps some remarks are in order concerning definition
3.4.1
. One thing that the reader might immediately notice is that the functors
-\odot M\colon^{Y}\mathbb{D}_{1}\to{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}
and
M\odot-\colon\mathbb{D}_{1}^{X}\to\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Y}
are not required to be specifically
\lambda
-accessible. In order to elaborate on this, but also because the accessibility of fixed domain/codomain categories
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}
,

\mathbb{D}_{1}^{X}
will be of importance later on, we begin by making the following observation concerning fibrations between accessible categories.

Lemma 3.4.3
.

Suppose that
P\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{X}
is a
fibration where both categories
\mathcal{A},\mathcal{X}
and the functor
P
are accessible. Then
for any object
X\in\mathcal{X}
, the fiber
\mathcal{A}_{X}
of
P
above
X
is an accessible category.

Proof.

For any object
X\in\mathcal{X}
, the fiber
\mathcal{A}_{X}
of
P
above
X
can be seen as the following pullback

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{X}}

where
\mathbf{1}=\{*\}
is the terminal category and
p_{X}
denotes the functor that picks out
X\in\mathcal{C}
. It is clear that all limits and colimits
exist (and are just the object
*
) and
\mathbf{1}
is locally
\lambda
-presentable for every
\lambda
. It is furthermore not too hard to see that the
functor
p_{X}
preserves
connected
(co)limits, so in particular filtered colimits. Hence, we can apply the Limit Theorem for accessible
categories
[
MP89
, Thm. 5.1.6]
, taking into account that
P
being a fibration implies that the pullback is also a bi-pullback, to deduce that
\mathcal{A}_{X}
is an
accessible
category. The same works for
P
an opfibration, since the crucial ingredient for the pullback to coincide with the bi-pullback is that
P
be an

iso
fibration.
∎

If we apply this observation to the context of a locally presentable double category, we deduce the following, for the fixed-domain/codomain subcategories
of
\mathbb{D}_{1}
.

Proposition 3.4.4
.

Suppose that
\mathbb{D}
is a locally presentable double category. Then for every
X,Y\in\mathbb{D}_{0}
the categories
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}
,

\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Y}
and
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Y}=\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})(X,Y)
are locally presentable.

Proof.

The categories
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}
and

\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Y}
are fibers of the (op)fibrations
\mathfrak{s}\colon\mathbb{D}_{1}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
and
\mathfrak{t}\colon\mathbb{D}_{1}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
respectively. Since
\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}
are cocontinuous,
Lemma

3.4.3
shows that both categories are accessible, while in addition being cocomplete by
3.1.13
.

Similarly, the category
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Y}
can be viewed as a fiber of the restricted source opfibration
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{D}_{1}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
(see
Proposition

3.1.8
). If
\lambda
is a regular cardinal for which both
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}
and
\mathbb{D}_{1}
are
\lambda
-accessible, then the inclusion
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{D}_{1}
is
\lambda
-accessible because it preserves all connected colimits by (the dual of)
Corollary

2.2.3
. Thus, the composite
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
is
\lambda
-accessible and the same arguments as above apply.
∎

As an example, we establish that categories of the form
{}^{X}\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{1}
and
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{1}^{Y}
are locally
\lambda
-presentable when
\mathcal{V}
is, and we also recover the well-known fact that
the categories
{}^{X}\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{1}^{Y}=\mathcal{V}^{X\times Y}
are locally
\lambda
-presentable (
[
AR94
, Corollary 1.54]
).

Remark 3.4.5
.

Notice that if
\mathbb{D}
is locally
\lambda
-presentable it does not follow that the categories
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}
,

\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Y}
and
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Y}
are themselves locally
\lambda
-presentable for the same
\lambda
. This is because the proof of
3.4.4
relies on
3.4.3
, whose proof in turn uses the Limit Theorem for
accessible
categories and in which the index of accessibility
\lambda
is not invariant. On the other hand, the Limit Theorem for locally presentable categories (in which
\lambda
remains fixed) cannot be applied because the functor
\mathbf{1}\to\mathcal{X}
does not preserve arbitrary (co)limits.

Coming back to the definition of locally
\lambda
-presentable double category in
3.4.1
, it seems reasonable that one could choose to require that all categories
{}^{X}\mathbb{D}_{1}
and
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Y}
are also locally
\lambda
-presentable and then that the functors
-\odot M
and
M\odot-
are all
\lambda
-accessible. We opted against this choice for two main reasons. Firstly, on a more practical level, the specific cardinal
\lambda
does not really play a role in the main results of this paper. Secondly, we felt that such considerations would lead in the direction of a general theory of accessible double categories, which is beyond the scope of the current paper and best left for future work. By the same token, we do not require the functor
\mathbf{1}\colon\mathbb{D}_{0}\to\mathbb{D}_{1}
to be accessible, even though that would again be a natural condition to consider and indeed holds for
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
.

As far as we are concerned in the present paper, the most important aspect of
Definition

3.4.1
lies in the fact that it manages to capture the example of
\mathbb{D}=\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
of
Example

3.1.2
. We particularly
thank Steve Lack for the first step of the proof below.

Proposition 3.4.8
.

Suppose that
\mathcal{V}
is locally presentable with colimits which are preserved by
\otimes
in each variable. Then the double category
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
is locally presentable.

Proof.

Suppose that
\mathcal{V}
is locally

\lambda
-presentable. Of course
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{0}=\mathsf{Set}
is locally
\lambda
-presentable, but we furthermore have a pullback square as follows:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Fam}(\mathcal{V})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Set}^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Set}.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\times}

The bottom functor is a
\lambda
-accessible right adjoint, while the right vertical
\mathsf{Fam}(\mathcal{V})\to\mathsf{Set}
has both a left and a right
adjoint
and the category
\mathsf{Fam}(\mathcal{V})
is itself locally
\lambda
-presentable. In addition,
\mathsf{Fam}(\mathcal{V})\to\mathsf{Set}
is an isofibration, which
implies that the pullback is also a bipullback. Thus, by the Limit Theorem for locally presentable categories (e.g.
[
AR94
, Ex. 2.l]
or
[
Bir84
, Thm. 2.18]
) we deduce that
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{1}
is locally
\lambda
-presentable and the two pullback projections are
\lambda
-accessible right adjoints. The
latter implies in particular that both
\mathfrak{s}
,
\mathfrak{t}
are themselves
\lambda
-accessible right adjoints. Furthermore, by
Proposition

3.1.10
we know that
\mathfrak{s}
and
\mathfrak{t}
preserve all colimits.

}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-3.1597pt}{0.87154pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform=matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -4.37 1.21)} \pgfsys@hbox{58}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
}\lxSVG@closescope }{{{{}{}{{}}
}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{{{}{}{{}}
}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{{{}{}{{}}
}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{{}}
}{{}{}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{}{}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{{{}{}{{}}
}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}

\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope }
\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}Z
, the
functor
M\odot-\colon\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{1}^{Y}\to\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{1}^{Z}
preserves filtered colimits. This follows from the description of colimits in such fibers
established in
3.1.15
and the following sequence of isomorphisms

\displaystyle M\odot C(z,x)

\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{y\in Y}M(z,y)\otimes C(y,x)\cong\sum\limits_{y\in Y}\left(M(z,y)\otimes\Big(\mathrm{Colim}_{i}\sum\limits_{q_{i}(x_{i})=x}Di(y,x_{i})\Big)\right)

\displaystyle\cong\sum\limits_{y\in Y}\left(\mathrm{Colim}_{i}\Big(M(z,y)\otimes\sum\limits_{q_{i}(x_{i})=x}Di(y,x_{i})\Big)\right)\cong\sum\limits_{y\in Y}\mathrm{Colim}_{i}\left(\sum\limits_{q_{i}(x_{i})=x}M(z,y)\otimes Di(y,x_{i})\right)

\displaystyle\cong\mathrm{Colim}_{i}\sum\limits_{q_{i}(x_{i})=x}\sum\limits_{y\in Y}\Big(M(z,y)\otimes Di(y,x_{i})\Big)\cong\mathrm{Colim}_{i}\sum\limits_{q_{i}(x_{i})=x}(M\odot Di)(z,x_{i})

and the latter is precisely the value of
\mathrm{Colim}_{i}(M\odot Di)
at
(z,x)
.

A similar calculation is valid for the functors
-\odot M\colon{}^{Z}\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{1}\to{}^{Y}\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{1}
.
∎

Proposition 3.4.9
.

Suppose that
\mathbb{D}
is a locally presentable double category. Then the category
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
is also locally presentable.

Proof.

As already observed in
Remark

3.1.12
for any fibrant
\mathbb{D}
,
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
can be viewed as the following pullback

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{0}\times\mathbb{D}_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\rangle}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Delta}

In this square we observe first of all that the diagonal functor
\Delta\colon\mathbb{D}_{0}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}\times\mathbb{D}_{0}
is accessible and has a left
adjoint, the latter because
\mathbb{D}_{0}
has binary coproducts. Similarly,
\langle\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}\rangle
is accessible and has a left adjoint because
both
\mathfrak{s}
and
\mathfrak{t}
have left adjoints and
\mathbb{D}_{1}
has binary coproducts. Thus, the
Limit
Theorem for locally presentable categories applies to yield that

\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}
is locally presentable, while the inclusion functor
\mathbb{D}_{1}^{\bullet}\to\mathbb{D}_{1}
(the top horizontal map in the
pullback) is an accessible right adjoint. ∎

As an example, in the case of
\mathbb{D}=\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
, the above proposition provides an elegant argument proving the fact that the category of
\mathcal{V}
-graphs and
\mathcal{V}
-graph homomorphisms
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Grph}
is a locally presentable category
when
\mathcal{V}
is, see
[
KL01
, Prop. 4.4]
.

We close up this section with a central result, that exhibits the effectiveness of the new parts of the theory on locally presentable double categories (
Definition

3.4.1
) and monoidal closed double categories (
Definition

3.2.9
) discussed in these past few sections. In more detail, we re-establish the main
[
Vas19
, Theorems 3.23 & 3.24]
in a broader context, dropping technical conditions that previously needed to be verified by hand in each specific double category of interest.

Theorem 3.4.12
.

(Sweedler theory of (co)monads)

be a braided monoidal closed double category, which is locally presentable.

Remark 3.4.13
.

Although at first sight, the braiding of
\mathbb{D}
is not needed for the second part of the above proof (also according to
Remark

2.3.10
), it is actually needed for the fact that
H^{\mathrm{op}}
has a parameterized adjoint
H
for the ordinary braided monoidal closed category
\mathbb{D}_{0}
.

The corollary below recovers
[
Vas19
, Theorems 4.37 & 4.38]
in a straightforward way, without the extra verifications needed therein.

Corollary 3.4.14
.

Suppose that
\mathcal{V}
is a symmetric monoidal closed category which is locally presentable. The category
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Cat}
is tensored and cotensored enriched in the braided monoidal closed
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Cocat}
, and the fibration
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Cat}\to\mathsf{Set}
is enriched in the monoidal opfibration
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Cocat}\to\mathsf{Set}
.

Proof.

Under the above assumptions, the double category
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
of
\mathcal{V}
-matrices is fibrant by
Example

3.1.7
, braided (in fact symmetric) monoidal by
Example

3.2.2
, monoidal closed by
Example

3.2.12
and locally presentable by
Proposition

3.4.8
. Hence all clauses of
Theorem

3.4.12
hold, and the results follow.
∎

Remark 3.4.15
.

A toy example where the conditions of
3.4.12
are also satisfied is given by the double category
\mathbb{R}\mathsf{el}(\mathsf{Set})
. Recall by
3.3.2
that
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{R}\mathsf{el}(\mathsf{Set}))
is the category
\mathsf{Preord}
of preordered sets and monotone functions. On the other hand, objects of
\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{R}\mathsf{el}(\mathsf{Set}))
are sets with a given subset, while morphisms are functions which map the prescribed subset of their domain inside the corresponding subset of their codomain. Now the enrichment of monads in comonads says something very easy and natural.

Remark 3.4.16
.

Following
Remarks

3.3.9
and
3.3.12
, the (one-object,one-vertical map) case of
Theorem

3.4.12
states that for a symmetric monoidal category
\mathcal{V}
which is monoidal closed and
locally presentable (since by
Definitions

3.2.9
and
3.4.1
these structures are directly inherited by the ordinary category of arrows which here becomes
\mathcal{V}
),
the category of monoids is tensored and cotensored enriched in the category of comonoids, namely
Theorem

2.3.2
.

On the other hand, the well-known fact that an one-object
\mathcal{V}
-category ‘is’ precisely a monoid in
\mathcal{V}

highlights a slightly different aspect of these one- versus many-object cases we have so far discussed: in the context of the double
category
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
, the tensored and cotensored enrichment of specifically
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Cat}=\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at})
in the symmetric monoidal

\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Cocat}=\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at})
of
Corollary

3.4.14
is indeed a many-object generalization of
Theorem

2.3.2
for a fixed monoidal category
\mathcal{V}
.

This discussion also propagates in the context of modules, as explained in the analogous
Remark

4.2.6
.

4.
Modules and comodules in double categories

This chapter begins, in
Section

4.1
, by setting up the general double categorical framework for modules and comodules, determining
their key categorical properties and obtaining results that shall be of use in what follows. The setting of
\mathcal{V}
-matrices continues to be the leading example.
Some important results include
Proposition

4.1.7
which renders both categories of (co)modules (co)monadic over specific pullback categories,
Propositions

4.1.10
and
4.1.12
where (op)fibration structures of (co)modules over (co)monads and objects are established in the fibrant setting,
and
Propositions

4.1.21
and
4.1.22
verifying these (op)fibrations are monoidal.

In
Section

4.2
, we turn to more specific structures that induce an enriched fibration of modules over monads in comodules over comonads, in a general double categorical setting under certain suitable conditions. The central
Theorem

4.2.4
which establishes the enrichment of modules in comodules is what we could refer to as ‘Sweedler theory for (co)modules’ in double categories,
providing a vast generalization of
Theorems

2.3.5
and
2.3.14
for monoidal categories.
Corollary

4.2.5
and
Remark

4.2.7
discuss the examples of enriched modules and comodules, in the context of enriched matrices.

4.1.
Basic constructions

Analogously to monads in double categories (
Definition

3.3.1
), modules in double categories as objects coincide with those in their horizontal
bicategory (
Definition

2.1.2
), whereas the morphisms between them are more general than their bicategorical counterpart.

These form the
global category of (left) modules
, denoted by
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
for any double category
\mathbb{D}
.

The terminology ‘left module’ comes of course from writting the action as
\lambda\colon A\odot M\Rightarrow M
. Notice that
bimodules
in the
setting of fibrant double categories appeared in
[
Shu08
, § 11]
, where it was shown that they are the horizontal 1-cells of a fibrant
double category of monads (therein called monoids), under certain assumptions on
\mathbb{D}
. In our context, we work with one-sided modules as defined above, in a general (and not
necessarily fibrant) double category.

We can consider a subcategory
{}_{A}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
of left
A
-modules for a fixed monad
A
, where morphisms are of the form
{}^{g}\zeta^{\mathrm{id}}
and have as
underlying monad map the identity.
Another subcategory of interest is
{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
of modules of arbitrary monads, but with fixed domain
U
, and the corresponding module morphisms
are now of the form
{}^{\mathrm{id}}\zeta^{f}
.
Finally, there is a subcategory
{}^{U}_{A}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
with objects all
A
-modules for a monad
A
and with fixed source

U
, and morphisms globular 2-cells. This category coincides with the category of modules in the horizontal bicategory
\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})
as seen
in
Definition

2.1.2
, which by
Remark

2.1.3
is the category of Eilenberg-Moore algebras for the ordinary
‘post-composition with
A
’ monad on the hom-category
\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})(U,X)={}^{U}\mathbb{D}_{1}^{X}
.

We usually denote a left
C
-comodule
(K,\gamma)
as
K_{C}
. A
comodule morphism

K_{C}\to L_{D}
consists of a comonad morphism
{}^{f}\alpha^{f}\colon C\to D
along with a 2-morphism

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\phi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L}

that satisfies a coaction compatibility condition dual to
37
.
We thus have the
global category of (left) comodules
, denoted by
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
for any double category
\mathbb{D}
.

As for modules, by fixing the comonad or the domain of the comodules or both, we respectively obtain categories
{}_{C}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
,

{}^{V}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
and
{}^{V}_{C}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
. The latter coincides with the category of comodules in the horizontal bicategory
\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})
,
namely
the category of Eilenberg-Moore coalgebras for the comonad ‘post-composition with
C
’ on the hom-category
\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})(V,Z)={}^{V}\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}
.

Remark 4.1.3
.

Similarly to
Remark

3.3.9
, in the (one-object,one-vertical arrow) case of a double category, the concepts of a module and a comodule
reduce to ordinary (left) modules and comodules over some monoid and comonoid in a monoidal category. We will later see that appropriate structure (e.g. monoidal) of the double category
also passes onto the categories of modules and comodules, in an analogous way as for monads and comonads of
Section

3.3
, hence also reduce to respective well-known facts in monoidal categories of

Section

2.1
.

\gamma_{z,v}\colon K(z,v)\longrightarrow\sum_{z^{\prime}\in Z}C(z,z^{\prime})\otimes K(z^{\prime},v)

satisfying coassociativity and counitality; since structure maps are now landing on sums, the axioms cannot be written precisely dual to
38
, rather
they become more involved as in

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K(z,v)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sum\limits_{z^{\prime}\in Z}C(z,z^{\prime}){\otimes}K(z^{\prime},v)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sum\limits_{z^{\prime\prime}\in Z}C(z,z^{\prime\prime}){\otimes}K(z^{\prime\prime},v)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sum\limits_{z^{\prime},z^{\prime\prime}\in Z}C(z,z^{\prime}){\otimes}C(z^{\prime},z^{\prime\prime}){\otimes}K(z^{\prime\prime},v)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma_{z,v}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma_{z,v}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sum 1\otimes\gamma_{z^{\prime},v}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sum\delta\otimes 1}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K(z,v)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sum\limits_{z^{\prime}\in Z}C(z,z^{\prime}){\otimes}K(z^{\prime},v)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\phantom{\sum\limits_{zZ}}}I{\otimes}K(z,v)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma_{z,v}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sum\epsilon\otimes 1}

using that
\otimes
preserves coproducts in both variables. With the respective notion of comodule morphism, we denote this category as
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at})
, whereas the special case where the domain is the singleton is denoted as
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Comod}
.

The following result, generalizing
Proposition

2.1.5
, shows that the global category of modules in any double category can naturally be expressed as the category of algebras over an
appropriate pullback of the category of arrows and the category of monads.

Proposition 4.1.7
.

The functor
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathbb{D}_{1}\times_{\mathbb{D}_{0}}\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
mapping
M_{A}
to the pair
(M,A)
is monadic. Dually, the functor

\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathbb{D}_{1}\times_{\mathbb{D}_{0}}\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})
mapping
K_{C}
to
(K,C)
is comonadic.

We next prove that there is a natural bijection between morphisms
F(M,A)\to N_{B}
in
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
and morphisms
(M,A)\to(N,B)
in

\mathbb{D}_{1}\times_{\mathbb{D}_{0}}\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
. By first considering such a morphism
(\phi,\alpha)
in the latter category, namely a pair of a 2-morphism

{}^{f}\phi^{g}\colon M\Rightarrow N
and a monad morphism
{}^{g}\alpha^{g}\colon A\Rightarrow B
, we obtain a module morphism
\bar{\phi}\colon(A\odot M)_{A}\to N_{B}
with underlying monad map
\alpha

Note that by the above, the unit of the adjunction has components
\eta_{(M,A)}\colon(M,A)\to(A\odot M,A)
given by pairs

(\eta_{A}\odot\rm{id}_{M},\rm{id}_{A})
.

Now consider an algebra for the monad induced by the above adjunction, namely a pair
(M,A)\in\mathbb{D}_{1}\times_{\mathbb{D}_{0}}\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
equipped with a
pair of a 2-morphism and a monad morphism
(\lambda\colon A\odot M\Rightarrow M,\beta\colon A\Rightarrow A)
. The unit axiom for the algebra shows
in particular that
\beta=\rm{id}_{A}
. Then the remainder of the two algebra axioms translate precisely to the fact that
\lambda\colon A\odot M\Rightarrow M
is an action making
M
into an
A
-module. Similarly, the property of
(\phi,\alpha)\colon(M,A)\to(N,B)
being an algebra morphism
is then precisely the statement that this pair defines a morphism in
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
.
∎

Proposition 4.1.9
.

Given any object
U
in a double category
\mathbb{D}
, the forgetful functor
{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to{}^{U}\mathbb{D}_{1}\times_{\mathbb{D}_{0}}\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
is
monadic. Dually,
{}^{V}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})\to{}^{V}\mathbb{D}_{1}\times_{\mathbb{D}_{0}}\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})
is comonadic.

The results so far concern modules in general double categories. Moving to the
setting of fibrant double categories, we can establish certain natural fibration
structures that involve categories of fixed monad or domain modules as follows.

∎

In fact, both structures above have sub(op)fibrations involving the fixed-domain (co)module categories in the following sense.

Proposition 4.1.11
.

Suppose
\mathbb{D}
is a fibrant double category. For any 0-cell
U
in
\mathbb{D}
,

{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
is a fibration and dually
{}^{V}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})
is an opfibration.

Proof.

This follows from the fact that the category

{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\subseteq\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})

is closed under cartesian liftings over
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
.
Indeed, as is clear from the above proof, the reindexing functors

\widecheck{f}\odot\textrm{-}
restrict between the subcategories

{}_{A}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\subseteq{}_{A}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
and
{}_{B}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\subseteq{}_{B}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
of the fibres with fixed domain

U
.
∎

Propositions

4.1.10
and
4.1.11
establish
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
and
{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
as fibred over
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
mapping a module to
its monad, and dually for the opfibrations mapping a comodule to its comonad. However, we can also view
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
and
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
as fibred over

\mathbb{D}_{0}
, and in fact in more than one ways, as can be seen below.

Proposition 4.1.12
.

Suppose
\mathbb{D}
is a fibrant double category. The source and target functors

\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\rightrightarrows\mathbb{D}_{0}
are a bifibration and a fibration respectively, and the source
and target functors
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})\rightrightarrows\mathbb{D}_{0}
are a bifibration and an opfibration respectively.

has domain the

and
similarly the lifting itself is a family of identity morphisms.

Under the assumption of fibrancy on
\mathbb{D}
, one can use the earlier monadicity results to easily deduce (co)completeness for categories of
(co)modules.

Proposition 4.1.15
.

Let
\mathbb{D}
be a fibrant double category which is parallel complete. Then
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
is complete and both forgetful functors

\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
and
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathbb{D}_{1}
preserve limits.

Proof.

Recall by
Definition

3.1.9
that both
\mathbb{D}_{0}
,
\mathbb{D}_{1}
are complete categories and that
\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{t}
are continuous functors.
We know by
Proposition

4.1.7
that
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
is monadic over
\mathbb{D}_{1}\times_{\mathbb{D}_{0}}\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
, hence has any
limits that the latter category has. Observe furthermore that, since
\mathfrak{t}
is a fibration in the fibrant setting, the pullback

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{1}\times_{\mathbb{D}_{0}}\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{s}/\mathfrak{t}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{t}}

is also a bi-pullback. Thus, since both
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
(
Proposition

3.3.6
) and
\mathbb{D}_{1}
have limits and
the functors
\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
(
Corollary

3.3.7
) and
\mathbb{D}_{1}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
preserve them, we deduce that
\mathbb{D}_{1}\times_{\mathbb{D}_{0}}\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
has all
small limits and that the functors
\mathbb{D}_{1}\times_{\mathbb{D}_{0}}\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
and
\mathbb{D}_{1}\times_{\mathbb{D}_{0}}\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathbb{D}_{1}

preserve them (e.g. by
[
BKP89
, Thm. 2.6]
). ∎

Combining the above with the fact that
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
is a fibration by
Proposition

4.1.10
, we obtain the following.

Corollary 4.1.16
.

Let
\mathbb{D}
be a parallel complete and fibrant double category. Then the fibration
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
has all small fibred limits.

Proof.

By
4.1.15
we have that the total category
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
has all small limits and that these are preserved by the functor

\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
. The result then follows from
2.2.2
. In particular, this says that all fibers
{}_{A}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
are complete and that
the reindexing functors
\widecheck{f}\odot\textrm{-}
are continuous functors.
∎

Similarly, we obtain the following results for comodules.

Proposition 4.1.17
.

Let
\mathbb{D}
be a fibrant double category which is parallel cocomplete. Then
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
is cocomplete,
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathbb{D}_{1}
preserves colimits and
the opfibration
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})
has all small opfibred colimits.

Proof.

The arguments are dual to those from above. In particular, for the cocomplete
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})
, the fiber categories
{}_{C}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
are cocomplete and the reindexing functors
\widehat{f}\odot\textrm{-}
are cocontinuous.
∎

\mathbb{D}

, where the monad is

. The latter

), both because the double category

.

,

\mathbb{D}
.

3.4.4
since as mentioned in the beginning of this section,
{}^{U}_{A}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
and
{}^{V}_{C}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
are
categories of Eilenberg-Moore algebras and coalgebras on the hom-categories
{}^{U}\mathbb{D}_{1}^{X}
and
{}^{V}\mathbb{D}_{1}^{Z}
respectively.
∎

Notice that the above generalizes the first part of
Proposition

2.1.9
, whereas the respective result for the global category of (co)modules is work in progress.

, we can

\mathbb{D}
.

Proposition 4.1.20
.

If
\mathbb{D}
is a monoidal double category, then the categories
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
and
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
inherit a monoidal structure from
\mathbb{D}_{1}
.

\mathbb{D}
is.

(A\otimes B)\odot(M\otimes N)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(\ref{eq:monoidaldoubleiso})}}{{\cong}}(A\odot M)\otimes(B\odot N)\xrightarrow{\lambda\otimes\lambda}(M\otimes N)

and the monoidal unit is

. Notice how this monoidal structure does not
restrict to any of the fixed domain or fixed monad module categories in a
straightforward way, since in return it provides functors

(43)

^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\times{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to{}^{U\otimes U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\quad\textrm{ and }\quad_{A}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\times{}_{A}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to{}_{A\otimes A}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D}).

By
Proposition

3.3.11
, in a fibrant monoidal double
category
\mathbb{D}
the categories of monads and comonads form a monoidal
fibration and opfibration respectively, above the
category of objects. For modules and comodules, we have the following analogous
result for the (op)fibration of (co)modules over (co)monads established in

Proposition

4.1.10
.

Proposition 4.1.21
.

If
\mathbb{D}
is a fibrant (braided/symmetric) monoidal double category, the fibration

\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
and opfibration
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})
are (braided/symmetric) monoidal.

Proof.

To verify
Definition

2.3.6
, first notice that all involved categories inherit their monoidal product from
\mathbb{D}
. By
construction, the underlying monad of
M_{A}\otimes N_{B}
is
A\otimes B
, the tensor of
the underlying monads, hence both functors are strict monoidal. Moreover, the
tensor preserves cartesian liftings: indeed, consider monad morphisms

{}^{f}\alpha^{f}\colon A^{\prime}\to A
and
{}^{g}\beta^{g}\colon B^{\prime}\to B
and modules

M_{A}
and
N_{B}
. Then the pair of cartesian liftings
\mathrm{Cart}(\alpha,M)
and

\mathrm{Cart}(\beta,N)
given in
41
gets tensored as the top arrow below

\textstyle{(\widecheck{f}\odot M)\otimes(\widecheck{g}\odot N)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\hskip 16.38895pt\hskip 8.19447pt\mathrm{Cart}(\alpha,M)\otimes\mathrm{Cart}(\beta,N)}
\scriptstyle{\cong}
\textstyle{M\otimes N\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{\widecheck{(f\otimes g)}\odot(M\otimes N)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\hskip 8.19447pt\mathrm{Cart}(\alpha\otimes\beta,M\otimes N)}
\textstyle{\textrm{in }\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})}
\textstyle{A^{\prime}\otimes B^{\prime}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\alpha\otimes\beta}
\textstyle{A\otimes B}
\textstyle{\textrm{in
}\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})}

The vertical isomorphism on the left-hand side is the
interchange isomorphism composed with the canonical
isomorphism
\widecheck{f}\otimes\widecheck{g}\cong\widecheck{f\otimes g}
in any fibrant double category. It then follows that the triangle in the above diagram commute,
and thus
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
is a monoidal fibration. Braiding and symmetry are easily verified to agree with the structure.

Dual arguments establish that
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})
is a monoidal opfibration.
∎

Using a similar methodology, we can also verify that the source bifibrations of
(co)modules over the category of objects are
monoidal.

It was mentioned above that fixed-domain module categories are not monoidal in general, since
the tensor product functor induces functors between modules with different
domains as in
43
. For our purposes, we investigate
certain assumptions under which fixed-domain (co)module categories of monoidal double categories do inherit the
tensor product.

Lemma 4.1.23
.

If
\mathbb{D}
is a fibrant double category and
T\cong U
as objects in
\mathbb{D}_{0}
, then there is an (adjoint) equivalence between the respective categories of
fixed-domain modules
{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\simeq{}^{T}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
.

Proof.

If
f\colon T\xrightarrow{\sim}U
is the vertical isomorphism, then the induced functor

\textrm{-}\odot\widehat{f}\colon{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to{}^{T}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
is an (adjoint) equivalence with adjoint
\textrm{-}\odot\widecheck{f}
, essentially because
\widehat{f}\dashv\widecheck{f}
is an adjoint
equivalence in the horizontal bicategory by
Lemma

3.1.5
, namely
\widehat{f}\odot\widecheck{f}\cong 1_{U}
and
\widecheck{f}\odot\widehat{f}\cong 1_{T}
via globular 2-cells in
\mathbb{D}_{1}
.
∎

Using this equivalence, we can restrict the tensor product functor accordingly
and obtain the following result for modules with domain the monoidal

and the

\diamond\colon{}^{I}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\times{}^{I}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\xrightarrow{\lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{eq:restrictedtensor}}{}^{I\otimes I}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\simeq{}^{I}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})

where the equivalence is
\textrm{-}\odot\widecheck{\rho_{I}}
. It can be verified this is a monoidal structure, where for example the left
unitor
I\diamond M\cong M
is built as

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I\otimes I}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\otimes I}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widecheck{\rho_{I}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\stackrel{{\scriptstyle q_{2}}}{{\cong}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rho_{M}}}{{\cong}}}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M\otimes 1_{I}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{X}}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1_{I}}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}

where the structure 2-morphism
q_{2}
of the conjoint of
\rho_{I}
is invertible by
Lemma

3.1.5
and the right hand side isomorphism is the right unitor of the
monoidal double category
\mathbb{D}
.

For the braiding or symmetry,
we can build a braiding as in

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I\otimes I}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\otimes Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I\otimes I}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y\otimes X}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widecheck{\rho_{I}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M\otimes N}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\tau}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widecheck{\rho_{I}}}
\scriptstyle\bullet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N\otimes M}

where
\tau
is the braiding of
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
and the left-hand side isomorphism comes from the axioms the monoidal category
\mathbb{D}_{0}
.
Using analogous arguments,
{}^{I}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
can be shown to be monoidal.
∎

Regarding an arbitrary object
U
as the fixed domain, one could consider
precomposition along companions or conjoints of some appropriate vertical map
U\otimes U\rightleftarrows U
to obtain composite functors

{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\times{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\xrightarrow{\otimes}{}^{U\otimes U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
in an effort to construct a tensor product in some coherent way.
It turns out that in a certain class of monoidal double categories, fixed-domain modules and comodules always
inherit a monoidal structure like that.

Proposition 4.1.25
.

Suppose that
\mathbb{D}
is a fibrant monoidal double category, whose category of objects
is cartesian monoidal
(\mathbb{D}_{0},\times,1)
. Then all fixed-domain module
and comodule categories
{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
and
{}^{V}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
for arbitrary objects
U,V
are monoidal. Moreover, they are braided/symmetric if
\mathbb{D}
is.

Proof.

According to the so-called monoidal Grothendieck construction, since the source
fibration
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
is monoidal by
Proposition

4.1.22
,
[
MV20
, Thm. 3.13]
ensures that it
corresponds to a lax monoidal structure on the corresponding pseudofunctor

\mathbb{D}_{0}^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathsf{Cat}
which sends an object
U
to the category of fixed-domain modules
{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
and
a vertical map
f
to the functor
\textrm{-}\odot\widehat{f}
(see
Proposition

4.1.12
). The lax monoidal structure maps are precisely the functors
\phi_{U,T}\colon{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\times{}^{T}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to{}^{U\otimes T}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
discussed above, along with
\phi_{0}\colon\mathbf{1}\to{}^{I}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
choosing
1_{I}
.

If the base monoidal category
\mathbb{D}_{0}
is cartesian monoidal,
by
[
Shu08
, Thm. 12.7]
or
[
MV20
, Thm. 4.2]
the monoidal structure of the fibration further
corresponds to a monoidal structure on the fibres, via

{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\times^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to{}^{U\times U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\xrightarrow{\textrm{-}\odot\widehat{\Delta}}{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D}),\qquad\mathbf{1}\to{}^{1}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\xrightarrow{\textrm{-}\odot\widehat{!}}{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})

where
\Delta\colon U\to U\times U
is the diagonal and
!\colon U\to 1
the
unique map to the terminal object. Therefore in that case, all fixed-domain
module categories are indeed monoidal.

Analogous arguments hold for
{}^{V}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
, again using the monoidal source fibration
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
.
Finally, when
\mathbb{D}
is braided monoidal then so are the monoidal (op)fibrations in question,
hence again by
[
Shu08
, Thm. 12.7]
the fibers
{}^{U}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
and
{}^{V}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
become braided monoidal.
∎

The condition of the above proposition is satisfied, for example, in any cartesian double category in the sense of
[
Ale18
]
. Moreover, it holds in the case of
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
whose category of objects is just sets.

Corollary 4.1.26
.

Suppose that
\mathcal{V}
is a braided monoidal category with small coproducts preserved by
\otimes
in each variable. Then the categories of two-indexed modules and comodules
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at})
and
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at})
, as well as the categories
of enriched modules
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Mod}
and comodules
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Comod}
are monoidal.
If
\mathcal{V}
is symmetric monoidal, then so are all four categories of modules and comodules.

Proof.

Under the initial assumptions on
\mathcal{V}
, the double category
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
is fibrant and monoidal (
Examples

3.1.7
and
3.2.2
).
Hence the first part for the two-indexed (co)modules of
Example

4.1.5
follows from
Proposition

4.1.20
, and the second part follows from
Proposition

4.1.24
, for
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Mod}{=}{}^{1}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at})
and

4.2.
Enrichment of modules in comodules

We now turn towards the main goal of this work, namely establishing an enrichment of modules over monads in comodules over comonads, in the setting
of a fibrant monoidal double category which is moreover monoidal closed and locally presentable. Using results obtained in the previous section, we gradually
build up the theory required to apply
Theorems

2.3.1
and
2.3.13
in order to show that
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
is tensored and cotensored enriched in

\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
, and that the fibration
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
is enriched in the opfribration
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})
(
Theorem

4.2.4
). The techniques are
very analogous to those employed for the respective result including monads and comonads,
Theorem

3.4.12
.

\mathbb{D}

31

H

is an action of the category of comodules on the category of modules.

Proposition 4.2.1
.

Proposition 4.2.2
.

Suppose
\mathbb{D}
is a braided monoidal closed and fibrant double category. The total functor
H
on the top of

(48)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H}

preserves cartesian liftings, therefore makes
(H,H)
into a fibred 1-cell.

Proof.

The square commutes by definition of the functor
H
.
We will show that the top
H
preserves cartesian liftings in each variable separately, for the fibrations of
Proposition

4.1.10
. That’s enough since
cartesian liftings of a product of fibrations are pairs of liftings in each one, see
[
Bor94
, Prop. 8.1.14]
.
Recall that part of the definition of a monoidal closed double category (
Definition

3.2.9
) is a map of adjunctions

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{D}_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textrm{-}\otimes K}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{t}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bot}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{t}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(K,\textrm{-})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textrm{-}\otimes Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bot}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(Z,\textrm{-})}

for any horizontal arrow
K
with target
Z
. In the fibrant context,
\mathfrak{t}
is a fibration (
Proposition

3.1.8
)
and since right adjoints in
\mathsf{Cat}^{\mathbf{2}}
preserve cartesian liftings (see e.g.
[
Jac99
, Ex. 9.4.4]
),
we have that
H(K,\textrm{-})
does so: for any
N
with target
Y
and any vertical map
f\colon Y^{\prime}\to Y
, cartesian maps are mapped to cartesian
maps as follows

(49)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(K,\widecheck{f}\odot N)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widecheck{f}\odot N}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textrm{in }\mathbb{D}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widecheck{H(1_{Z},f)}\odot H(K,N)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(K,N)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textrm{in }\mathbb{D}_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textrm{in }\mathbb{D}_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(Z,Y^{\prime})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(Z,Y)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textrm{in }\mathbb{D}_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(1,\mathrm{Cart}(f,N))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\exists!u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cart}(f,N)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cart}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mapsto}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(1_{Z},f)}

Due to the nature of cartesian liftings for the fibration

given by

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(K,\textrm{-})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(K,\textrm{-})}

for any

-comodule

-module

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(K,\widecheck{f}\odot N)}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widecheck{H(1_{Z},f)}\odot H(K,N)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(K,N)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textrm{in }\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B^{\prime}_{Y^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textrm{in }\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(C,B^{\prime})}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cart}(\alpha,N)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Cart}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mapsto}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H(1_{C},\alpha)_{H(1_{Z},f)}}

that looks very similar to

but the base category is of horizontal 1-cells (and specifically monads) rather than 0-cells.
By the universal property of cartesian liftings in
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
, there exists a unique module map
k\colon H(K,\widecheck{f}\odot N)\to\widecheck{H(1,f)}\odot H(K,N)
that makes the triangle

First of all, we notice that

has the same domain and codomain

-isomorphism

from

. Then, the cartesian liftings of

given as the right side of

,
essentially because the former only employs the underlying vertical map of the monad maps involved. As a result, since

in

in particular means that
the equality holds in
\mathbb{D}_{1}
, and

is the unique map in
\mathbb{D}_{1}
that makes the same diagram commute there, the module map

is forced to be equal, as a horizontal 1-cell, to

and

is an isomorphism.

We now establish that the global category of comodules in a double category is monoidal closed under certain assumptions,
similarly to the category of comonads in
Proposition

3.4.11
. This generalizes
Proposition

2.3.3
from monoidal to double categories.

We have now set up all pieces in order to deduce that the fibration of modules over monads (
Proposition

4.1.10
) is
enriched in the monoidal opfibration of comodules over comonads (
Proposition

4.1.21
).
This is the (co)module analogue of the relevant result for (co)monads over the category of
objects, see
Theorem

3.4.12
. This result is the many-object generalization of
Theorems

2.3.5
and
2.3.14
, moving from monoidal categories to double categories.

Theorem 4.2.4
.

(Sweedler theory for (co)modules)
Let
\mathbb{D}
be a braided monoidal closed double category, which is fibrant and locally presentable.

(1)

The category of modules
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
is tensored and cotensored enriched in the category of comodules
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
.

(2)

The fibration
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
is enriched in the monoidal opfibration
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})
.

.

is braided monoidal when

Proposition

4.1.20
. Moreover,

is an action by

(2)
This follows by

. First of all, the opfibration

∎

Analogously to
Corollary

3.4.14
, the above theorem directly applies to the setting of enriched matrices, giving the desired enrichment of enriched modules in enriched comodules
in their most general form.

Corollary 4.2.5
.

Suppose that
\mathcal{V}
is a symmetric monoidal closed and locally presentable category. Then the category
\mathsf{Mod}(\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at})
of two-indexed
\mathcal{V}
-modules is tensored
and cotensored enriched in the category
\mathsf{Comod}(\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at})
of two-indexed
\mathcal{V}
-comodules.

Proof.

Recall the description of the involved categories from
Examples

4.1.5
and
4.1.6
. All clauses of
Theorem

4.2.4
are satisfied: under these assumptions,
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
is a braided (in fact symmetric) monoidal double category
by
Example

3.2.2
, fibrant by
Example

3.1.7
, monoidal closed as a double category by
Example

3.2.12
and also locally presentable by
Proposition

3.4.8
.
∎

Remark 4.2.6
.

Analogously to
Remark

3.4.16
and using
Remark

4.1.3
, the one-object case of the above theorem reduces to the enrichments that arise in the context of a symmetric monoidal closed (ordinary) category, i.e.

Theorems

2.3.5
and
2.3.14
. In more detail,
Theorem

4.2.4
states in particular that for a monoidal category –
namely a (one-object, one-vertical arrow) double category – which is symmetric monoidal closed and locally presentable, the global category of modules is tensored and cotensored enriched in the global category
of comodules, as well as the fibration of modules over monoids is enriched in the opfibration of comodules over comonoids.

Remark 4.2.7
.

We can also view
Corollary

4.2.5
as a many-object generalization of the enrichment of modules in comodules in a specific
\mathcal{V}
, using precisely
\mathbb{D}=\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
. In fact, if one wanted
to actually establish the enrichment of the category of
\mathcal{V}
-modules
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Mod}={}^{1}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at})
in the category of
\mathcal{V}
-comodules
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Comod}={}^{1}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at})
as those
were described in
Examples

4.1.5
and
4.1.6
, that would require a sub-case of
Theorem

4.2.4
that involves modules and comodules with fixed domains
11
11

11

The specific enrichment of enriched modules in enriched comodules is obtained in
[
Vas14
, Thm. 7.7.7]
in a more technical and less general way.
.

In a bit more detail, we would once again apply
Theorem

2.3.1
, this time to the composite functor

\tilde{H}\colon{}^{I}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})^{\mathrm{op}}\times{}^{I}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to{}^{H(I,I)}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\xrightarrow{\simeq}{}^{I}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})

where the first part is the functor
H
between the respective fibers and the second one is the (adjoint) equivalence induced, according to
Lemma

4.1.23
, by the standard isomorphism
I\cong H(I,I)
in
\mathbb{D}_{0}
. We know that
{}^{I}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
is braided monoidal by
Proposition

4.1.24
, and we can adjust
Proposition

4.2.1
to establish that
\tilde{H}
is an action: the structure isomorphisms
\psi_{1},\mu_{1}
would have a pasted 2-isomorphism on their left which would ‘normalize’ the domains of all horizontal 1-cells to
I
.

, one considers a square

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}^{I}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})}

where both legs are opfibrations by

4.1.11
, the top functor preserves cocartesian liftings using an argument
as for
50
which holds for arbitrary domain (co)modules, the bottom functor has an adjoint
P(\textrm{-},B)
and the composite functor between
the fibers is precisely
52
but now emanating from
{}^{\phantom{ABC}I}_{P(A,B)}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
and landing on
{}^{H(I,I)}_{\phantom{AB}A}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
. The domain is locally
presentable by
Proposition

4.1.18
and the restricted functors are still cocontinuous (since the fixed domains are of the ‘right shape’).
Theorem

2.2.1
then applies and produces the desired adjoint.

Hence the result follows and each
{}^{I}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
is enriched in
{}^{I}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
, giving the enrichment of
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Mod}
in
\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathsf{Comod}
as a particular case when
\mathbb{D}=\mathcal{V}\textrm{-}\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
.
For the existence of tensors and cotensors, we can adjust
Proposition

4.2.3
in order to show that
{}^{I}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
is monoidal closed, and also again work as in the proof of
Theorem

4.2.4
for the adjoint of
\tilde{H}(K,\textrm{-})
. Similarly for the enrichment of the fibration
{}^{I}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Mnd}(\mathbb{D})
in the monoidal opfibration
{}^{I}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})\to\mathsf{Cmd}(\mathbb{D})
. We don’t go into these details so as to not further prolong this already extended work.

Notice that the above arguments indicate that we can obtain enrichments of any
{}^{X}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
in the monoidal
{}^{I}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
using an appropriate functor

{}^{I}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})^{\mathrm{op}}\times{}^{X}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\to{}^{H(I,X)}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})\xrightarrow{\simeq}{}^{X}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})

since
{}^{X}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathbb{D})
being monoidal is not needed in the above arguments – but of course
{}^{I}\mathsf{Comod}(\mathbb{D})
being monoidal as the enriching base
is needed (
Proposition

4.1.24
).
